title: Mike Flanagan’s ‘Carrie’ Envisioned As Three Seasons In “Dream Scenario”
full_text: Skip to main content By Armando Tinoco Armando Tinoco Staff Writer @armietinoco More Stories By Armando ‘Dancing With The Stars’ Recap: Yacht Rock Night Sees One Couple Eliminated In Week 3 ‘Vanderpump Rules: Lisa Las Vegas’ Trailer & Episode Release Guide Schedule Set At Bravo Dennis Haskins Dies: ‘Saved By The Bell’s Mr. Belding Was 75 View All September 30, 2026 8:45am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Summer H. Howell Prime Video Mike Flanagan adapted Stephen King ‘s Carrie into a series, and in a “dream scenario,” he would like it to run as a trilogy. Already counting on King’s approval of the adaptation, Flanagan has a specific vision for Carrie that could potentially go beyond the original story. “In my dream scenario,” Flanagan said in an interview with Collider . “I think it’s three seasons. In my dream scenario, I think Carrie has a wonderful three-step arc. It’s a trilogy, really.” Carrie follows misfit high‑schooler Carrie White (Howell) after having spent her life hidden away inside the walls of her home with her fiercely protective mother, Margaret (Samantha Sloyan). Following her father’s unexpected death, Carrie enters the public high school ecosystem and is forced to navigate a viral bullying scandal that tears through her community. Watch on Deadline Related Stories Books 'The Love Hypothesis' Author To Release Book Sequel, MRC Developing Film Adaptation For Amazon News Amazon's Kelly Day Says AI Will Unlock "Creative Risk" & Help Free Up Creatives Working On The Next Big Hit Carrie also faces the relentless pressure and casual cruelty of the social‑media age, and the awakening of mysterious telekinetic powers that rise alongside her adolescence. The supernatural horror miniseries premieres on October 7 on Prime Video with Summer H. Howell in the title role. Carrie was first adapted into a film in 1976, with Brian De Palma directing a screenplay written by Lawrence D. Cohen and Sissy Spacek as Carrie. A direct sequel, directed by Katt Shea, The Rage: Carrie 2 was released in 1999, with Emily Bergl playing Rachel Lang, Carrie’s younger half-sister. In 2002, a television film directed by David Carson and based on a screenplay by Bryan Fuller debuted on NBC, with Angela Bettis as Carrie. Before the new miniseries on Prime Video, Kimberly Peirce directed a 2013 remake starring Chloë Grace Moretz. title: Being Clarissa Ward: CNN Star Speaks on Gaza, Trump — and Her Ellison-Era Future
full_text: × Skip to main content By Steven Zeitchik Plus Icon Steven Zeitchik Senior Editor, Technology and Politics View All September 30, 2026 8:45am CNN chief international correspondent Clarissa Ward attends the conversation as part of Warner Bros. Discovery WBD at Cannes Lions on June 23, 2022 in Cannes, France. Ward has been on the frontlines of foreign reporting lately, in multiple ways. Arnold Jerocki/Getty Images for Warner Bros. Discovery What’s more scary than being a lead international correspondent at a time of multiple brutal wars and violent online rhetoric? Being a lead international correspondent when the whole future of your network is entering uncertain ownership hands. As CNN ‘s chief international correspondent, Clarissa Ward may have one of the best jobs in all of media. But she also has one of the most fraught jobs in all of media. Dodging explosions in Ukraine, seeking an entree into Gaza, reporting from the Spanish-run city of Ceuta as migrants come pouring in from Morocco — Ward has been in every hotspot and then some recently. And all this before David Ellison got final approval to buy CNN along with the other assets of Warner Bros. Discovery. The Hollywood Reporter met the London-based Ward last week at a midtown Manhattan hotel on a rare recent trip to New York (she was here to see her bosses and meet with the president of Latvia, as one does). Not even 24 hours had passed since California attorney general Rob Bonta and other states settled their case against Ellison, clearing the way for him to own the cable-news giant. She had a few things to say about all of it. First, how are you feeling? About the state of the world but also the state of the news world. Oh it’s all great [laughs sarcastically]. No, I think I’m feeling really good about journalism. It’s hard, but there’s so much great work everywhere. As for the world… One of your biggest crusades has been about a place you can’t report from — Gaza. Are there signs that the Israeli government is changing its stance and will journalists have more access, as you and others have been pushing for? There’s a massive amount of pressure but not really. And we need to. What you can get now just isn’t enough. I don’t want wide shots of rubble — I want an old man in a chair telling me his story. And also I can’t report with the same moral authority if I’m not there. No one can. So that really needs to change. Iran seems to pose similar challenges right now. Totally. We mostly hear what the U.S. or Iran want us to hear, and the people of Iran lose when that happens. Everyone loses when that happens. There’s of course the fear that even if you get in to those places there’s a limit to what we can trust because a lot of Palestinians are still so afraid of Hamas and a lot of Iranians still so afraid of the regime. Does that concern you? Absolutely. In every conflict there’s self-censoring but in these two it’s worse in many ways . As we’re speaking there’s another kind of censoring effort going on right here in the U.S., with Trump banning CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House. How is that landing with you? It’s very concerning. But I think it’s also very encouraging to see the solidarity — look at what Fox News just did [in joining the other networks’ pool boycott]. Media companies realize a threat against some of us is a threat against all of us, even if they don’t agree on much else. What’s one place you’d like to be able to report from that you haven’t been allowed into recently? Sudan. It’s extremely hard, and Darfur is even harder. And the country [in the midst of a brutal 3+ year civil war] is in major crisis. What’s one place or story you have recently reported on that we’re not paying enough attention to? The migrant crisis in Europe. Being in Ceuta and seeing the migrants streaming across the border — this is part of a phenomenon that is going to change so much. Look at what just happened with AfD in Germany [ winning an election in Saxony-Anhalt] and how the migrant crisis plays into it. It’s affecting everything. You’ve tried to mix things up on social media lately, talking about journalism while having tea in your kitchen or pastries in an airport or just dancing through a train station to “Shake Your Groove Thing .” It’s a bit of a different path from what you and frankly many foreign correspondents have previously taken. At the beginning people were saying ‘this is weird’ and ‘what are you doing?’ But I feel we have to meet viewers where they are. Some institutions have become a little bit [pauses]…formal in how they report the news. [Lowers her voice to faux-seriousness for the next phrase] ‘Over these hills behind me, you can see’ — I mean, nobody talks like that anymore. Content creators talk the way viewers themselves talk. [Laughs] No certainly not, though there are some who say foreign correspondents should keep that formal tradition alive. And I get that. I wouldn’t do it if I was, say, reporting from Syria. We have to be careful not to cross any lines. But also I think it’s OK to ask ‘what if we tried something on for size, in the right context?’ ‘What if it feels looser, more like you’re listening to a friend?’ People don’t want to feel like they’re being bullshitted — young people especially but everybody. So I’m trying to do something so they don’t feel that way. Some people will see these videos and also wonder if you’re planning on a post-correspondent life. A few of your CNN colleagues have certainly had success outside the machine — Jim Acosta, Don Lemon. Is that something you can see yourself doing? They’ve done great but I’ve always loved being in the field, being out there reporting, and to do that [for broadcast] you really need an institution like CNN behind you. But nowadays you’d be unwise not to look at other things. I’m not going to pretend I know what that is [at this point]. But you have to look. A lot of tongues wagged when back in the spring you signed only a one-year contract instead of a long-term one. Was that a signal you may be preparing for an eventual life outside CNN, especially with a new owner coming in? There are so many things going on and you don’t want to rush into anything without a clear-eyed view in terms of how much is changing. So that’s where that was coming from. On the subject of that train video, you did get a clapback from the White House social media team, which derided you for doing it and called you a “hot mess,” among other lovely names. What was your reaction to that? I mean, we’re having fun. It’s social media. So much of content is people taking things out of boxes. It’s not like we were on CNN on the front page of the web site. I don’t know, I’m not sure why overt displays of joy make some people feel inadequate. THR

Paramount is awaiting one last step before it can close the $111 billion Warner Bros. title: Canada’s Banger Films Tunes Up Animated Rock Comedy ‘Gone To Hell’
full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Fremantle International Commercial Strategy VP Jill Kellie Exits After Four Years ‘Joseph’s Machines’, ‘Triple Charm’ & ‘What’s Up Moms’ Among Volt Factor Shows Rolling Out On Future Today Channels Hearst Networks UK Buys ‘American Chopper’ Revival Series ‘Orange County Choppers Original’ View All September 30, 2026 8:42am Add us as a Google Preferred Source EXCLUSIVE: Gone to Hell , a Canadian adult animation about a world-famous rock band who are sent to the underworld, will launch next month. The series, billed as “part supernatural adventure, part rock-and-roll sature, debuts on the BangerTV YouTube channel on October 30. Brian Peco and Craig Mailman are the co-creators and Banger Films is producing with support from the Independent Production Fund, Canada Media Fund and Ontario Creates. Robin Hatch comprised the music. Per the synopsis, the eight-episode series, set in 1994, follows Demon Destroyer, a world-famous rock band whose members are crushed by their own stage mascot during a live performance and sent straight to Hell. There’s just one complication: They aren’t actually dead. Related Stories Casting Lauren Cohan & Jake Epstein To Co-Star In Eric Stoltz-Directed Rom-Com 'Both Sides Now' News Canada's Precious Metal Productions & Black Fawn Distribution Strike Genre Slate Deal - TIFF Back on Earth, the band remain comatose and their predicament triggers an obscure rule of the underworld known as the Coma Clause, which keeps the Gates of Hell open to them for as long as their bodies remain alive. If they can reach the gates before their record label pulls the plug, they can return to Earth, or they will be stuck in this version of Hell, which isn’t particularly scary but populated by self-absorbed oddballs and ruled by the egomaniacal Dev, who has his own ambitions for fame. Watch on Deadline Voice cast includes Paul Spence ( FUBAR , Deaner 89’ ) as Demon Destroyer frontman Rick Fashun, Chris Locke as Dev Devilio, Derrick Beckles ( Hot Package , The Eric Andre Show ) as drummer Donnie, Jackie Pirico as bassist Jojo and Kevin Morgan as Derek, Dev’s assistant, and Deva, Dev’s sister. The show marks Banger Films’ first animated series. The company is best known for music and pop culture programs and films such as the Peabody and Emmy Award-winning Hip-Hop Evolution , Rush: Beyond the Lighted Stage and Metal: A Headbanger’s Journey . “Craig and I wanted to make something that captured the feeling of the cartoons we grew up watching every Saturday morning,” said Peco, the co-creator, writer, director and producer. “We created these hilarious characters, then we literally made Hell. The world is made up of miniature sets that I made and they became such an important part of the identity of the show. There’s an imperfection to it that makes this strange world feel real. The opposite of AI slop.” “ Gone To Hell started with this very simple idea of a rock band trying to escape Hell, but the more we developed it, the more it became a story about people who are never quite satisfied with what they have,” added Mailman, co-creator and producer. “It gave us a really funny foundation for the characters, but also a world that can keep getting bigger and stranger.” You can see a trailer above. title: Tribeca Festival Sets 2027 Dates, Submission Deadlines
full_text: × Skip to main content By Hilary Lewis Plus Icon Hilary Lewis Deputy Editor, East Coast hilarylewis Follow Sign Up View All September 30, 2026 8:41am The Tribeca Festival Dimitrios Kambouris/Getty Images After celebrating its landmark 25th anniversary edition, the Tribeca Festival isn’t going anywhere. The festival has announced that its 26th installment will take place from June 3-12, 2027. Submissions are now open across the festival’s programming categories: features, shorts and music videos, Tribeca TV, Tribeca digital creators, Tribeca games, Tribeca podcasts and Tribeca X. The 25th anniversary festival, which took place from June 3-14 earlier this year, featured a record 104 feature film world premieres and more than 240 live events. Highlights included Bruce Springsteen receiving the Harry Belafonte award and participating in a conversation and performance with Bono and Patti Smith as well as the premieres of Madonna’s Confessions II cinematic experience , a companion piece to her Confessions II album released in July; Katy Perry’s concert film The Lifetimes Tour: Live From Paris ; the Katie Holmes-Joshua Jackson rom-com Happy Hours , marking a much-anticipated onscreen reunion for the Dawson’s Creek stars; the all-AI Iran film Dreams of Violets ; and the compelling Margo Martindale-led trucker drama The Long Haul . Tribeca was built on the belief that the next great storyteller could come from anywhere, and we look forward to meeting the voices who will define the 2027 Festival.” Festival passes, including for the new Hudson Opening Weekend option, offering access to Festival programming from opening night through its first Monday, and, in its second year, an Under 25 pass, are now on sale. title: Former CW Bosses Dawn Ostroff and Mark Pedowitz Look Back at the Network’s First 20 Years
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Sep 30, 2026 8:30am PT Former CW Bosses Dawn Ostroff and Mark Pedowitz Look Back at the Network’s First 20 Years By Michael Schneider Plus Icon Michael Schneider Executive Editor franklinavenue Latest As the CW Turns 20, the Once YA-Focused Network Takes a Look at the Road Ahead 30 minutes ago ‘Jimmy Kimmel Live’ Kicks Off Broadcast’s Fall TV Premiere Week as No. 1 Show in Late Night (EXCLUSIVE) 24 hours ago CBS and MTV VMAs Attract a Combined 8.4 Million Viewers, Making it the Most-Watched Since 2015 and Up 51% From Last Year 2 days ago See All Katie Yu / Cate Cameron / Dean Buscher When Warner Bros. and CBS announced the merger of the WB and UPN on the morning of Jan. 24, 2006, the industry was shocked. There had been no rumblings that it might happen, as the two sides behind the deal somehow managed to keep it a secret. “Even then there weren’t many surprises that you could really pull off,” says Dawn Ostroff , who was president of UPN, and after the merger, became the CW ’s entertainment president. “Nobody expected it. Those two networks had been competitors for 10 years, going after the same audience and had really been at each other’s throat. People were astonished!” Related Stories Emmy Producers on Recruiting Taylor Swift, the Ideas She Brought to the Show and How This Year’s Telecast Wound Up Short ‘Charlie’s Angels’ Star Jaclyn Smith on the Emmys Reunion, ‘Snobbism’ Against the Series and Why the Latest Movie Reboot 'Didn't Work' Now, the CW has hit its 20th anniversary — living twice as long as its predecessors. And although the network has evolved under its new Nexstar ownership, for most of those first two decades the CW was known as the home for young adult-oriented series, including “Supernatural,” “Gossip Girl,” “The Vampire Diaries,” “Arrow,” “The Flash,” “One Tree Hill,” “Riverdale,” “Jane the Virgin,” “Crazy Ex-Girlfriend” and “All American” — which just wrapped as the final drama from that two-decade era. Popular on Variety “The CW was always a place where you knew that the people loved the stories they were telling, and loved the shows that they were putting up there,” says Greg Berlanti , who had as many as nine series on the air simultaneously on the network, including massive hits “Arrow” and “The Flash.” “I think we’ll talk about those years at the CW as being a bit of a magical time in this art form.” Ostroff oversaw the birth of the CW, starting with making the difficult decisions of which shows from the WB and UPN to carry over and which ones would have to be canceled. That first year was difficult, Ostroff recalls, as no one understood what “CW” meant (it was the first initials of CBS and Warner Bros., but everyone thought it was “Country/Western,” she recalls). “Here we were, having to formulate a new network that combined those two companies, figuring out a new culture and creating something that everybody would feel a part of. It was a real challenge,” she says. That included audience confusion, as viewers weren’t sure where to find their favorite WB and UPN shows anymore. In some markets, the WB affiliate became the CW, and in other cities, it was the local UPN station that made the transition. “People say, ‘You started at ground zero,’ but I always say, ‘We started about 100 feet below ground zero!’” Ostroff says. “Because between everyone not knowing what CW was and everyone trying to find their favorite shows on different channels, it was just mass chaos.” But then came “Gossip Girl,” which became one of the first homegrown CW success stories. The series made waves starting with its marketing campaign, which promoted the show with the phrase “OMFG” on billboards and in TV spots. “The Vampire Diaries” became a phenom as well — including a Season 4 premiere poster that suggested a ménage à trois between the main characters. “We just made a lot of noise and finally figured out like how we were going to let people know what the CW was,” Ostroff says. Ostroff left in 2011, and Mark Pedowitz took over as the CW president. He familiarized himself with the network’s series by watching every episode, reading every script and then flying across North America to visit producers and talent on sets and over dinners. “We were small enough to do that, and other platforms weren’t really doing that,” he says. “The first show we went up to see was ‘Supernatural.’ And then we just started booking trips wherever they were shooting, whether it be Albuquerque, Toronto, New Orleans, Atlanta. It created a connection.” A year after Pedowitz joined, the CW launched “Arrow” — which would soon turn into a sprawling franchise with “The Flash,” “Supergirl,” “DC’s Legends of Tomorrow,” “Black Lightning” and “Batwoman,” all from Berlanti and Warner Bros. TV. Greg Berlanti with his “Arrowverse” stars Grant Gustin, Melissa Benoist, Caity Lotz and Stephen Amell in 2016. FilmMagic “It allowed us to broaden out from a demographic point of view,” Pedowitz says. “We never lost the roots of who we were, with ‘The Vampire Diaries’ and the rest But [the “Arrowverse”] was huge because it said that our programming, despite whatever limitations we might had had, was as good as anybody else’s.” And although Emmy recognition remained elusive — a sore subject for Pedowitz, who’s still fired up about that snub — shows like “Jane the Virgin” and “Crazy Ex-Girlfriend,” both from CBS Studios, became critical faves and earned big Golden Globes wins. Neither show were ratings hits, but Pedowitz remembers being asked at the time why he kept both shows on the air: “I said, ‘I really like them and I can keep them on the air.’ And we did,” he says. “By the way, ‘Jane the Virgin’ worked extraordinarily well in streaming for us at the CW as well as for Netflix. ‘Crazy Ex-Girlfriend’ was very much a cult following, but it was so different, and no one’s really accomplished what [co-creator and star] Rachel Bloom did since then.” There’s a few that got away: “The Chilling Adventures of Sabrina” wound up at Netflix, and Pedowitz regrets not ordering the pilot “Haunted” to series. Plus, he now believes, “There was much more life left in ‘The Vampire Diaries’ universe.” Yet, the CW was able to survive and thrive thanks to its output deal with Netflix, which started in 2011 and allowed the network to become profitable through licensing. “We created a vibrant business,” Pedowitz says. “And we had the programming to make it vibrant.” That deal ended in 2019, as both CBS and Warner Bros. launched their own streaming services — and by 2022, both companies decided it was time to sell the CW to key affiliate partner Nexstar. Pedowitz looks back at his nearly 12 years running the CW with great memories. “It was the people. As the leader, you try to move it in the direction of the culture that you want to lead in,” he says. “But it’s all depending on the people. They create the culture.” And for 20 years, the CW viewers have agreed. Additional episodes will air in 2027. “Ted: The Animated” series was announced in May 2025 and is set 12 years after the events of “Ted” and “Ted 2.” As previously announced, Seth MacFarlane will once again voice the titular teddy bear come to life, with Mark Wahlberg, Amanda Seyfried and Jessica Barth reprising their film roles as John, Sam and Tami-Lynn, respectively. In addition, Kyle Mooney will voice the new character Apollo, while Liz Richman will voice Ruth. Follow these two lovable stoners as they enable each other’s bad ideas about marriage, parenting and the challenges of adult life.” Popular on Variety This is the second “Ted” TV series on Peacock. The streamer also aired a live-action prequel series set during John’s High School years for two seasons. MacFarlane executive produces via Fuzzy Door along with Erica Huggins, Alana Kleiman, Jason Clark, Aimee Carlson and Claudia Katz. The series is produced by Universal Global Television and MRC. title: ‘Unmasking a Monster’: Star, EP, and ID President on Using AI Masks to Perfect Their Aileen Wuornos Look
full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All September 30, 2026 8:15am Actress Morag Peacock before an AI mask made her look like Aileen Wuornos in 'Unmasking a Monster: Aileen Wuornos' Courtesy of Investigation Discovery You’ve never see Aileen Wuornos like this. Or perhaps it is more accurate to say you’ve seen her exactly like this. Investigation Discovery’s new documentary series Unmasking a Monster: Aileen Wuornos utilized an AI -mask tool in post-production to make actress Morag Peacock look exactly like the infamous serial killer. The docuseries then did the same with nine other actors and their real-life counterparts. This specific deployment of AI is a first for the industry, the series’ executive producer Stephen Dost told The Hollywood Reporter . The vice president of content at Arrow Media had been “aware” of the digital mask tech, which he describes as “really advanced motion capture” — Dost just needed a use case. “We were asking ourselves, ‘If you could show someone as they were at the time, what kind of story would make sense for that?'” Dost recalled. “I just kept coming back again and again to Aileen Wuornos, and probably the reason for that is that if you’re going to show someone’s face, there’s got to be a reason. It can’t be for the sake of showing off tech.” “With [Wuornos], if you look at her face, you can see the the suffering that went behind it. You can see the abuse that she went went through,” he continued. “It’s a bit like the story of her life you can read on her face, and she went through hell.” There were other reasons. For starters, archival footage of Wuornos is “very limited,” Dost said. Plus, traditional TV reenactments are flawed, ID president Jason Sarlanis told THR . “Audiences want realism and access to the truth behind these stories. Reenactments have been part of this genre from the start, but they’ve also been an obstacle to believability,” Sarlanis said. “By augmenting our actors’ performances with digital prosthetics, we can bring viewers into these key moments with a new level of authenticity.” “In a traditional reenactment, you would actually try to avoid [the actor’s] face. You would try to be abstract,” Dost said. “But this was an opportunity to look right at her — uncomfortably — at the humanity that was there.” Dost just needed a human with a face. OK, it was a bit more than that. The docuseries needed a capable actress that, with 90 minutes of hair and makeup (and one prosthetic tooth), could kind of look like Wuornos. “Where the tech was at the time, we needed someone who had basically the same face shape,” Dost said. Peacock’s face worked for the assignment. It was her eyes that did the heavy lifting. “We would get through a take, and you could hear a pin drop at the end. We’re not seeing any of the VFX — it felt like we were in the room with Aileen Wuornos,” Dost said. Peacock played it as if her own face would make the finished product. “I’m going for as close to her as possible, and then the the technology bit kind of left my head after that. I was like, ‘This is the job that I’m supposed to do. I’ll do mine to the best of my ability, and then after that, it’s over to them. Hopefully, they get what they want, and everyone’s happy,” she told THR . “So, I knew about it — it was probably there in the back of my mind, but it was more about…matching her mannerisms, her quirks, the way she expressed with her eyes and things like that.” Peacock says she was “pleasantly surprised” by the trailer, which is the first time she saw footage from the final cut. “I can definitely recognize myself underneath it,” Peacock said. Her family did too. Aileen Wuornos: The Selling of a Serial Killer, Aileen Wuornos, 1992. Strand Releasing/Courtesy Everett Collection. AI is Hollywood’s hottest-button issue this side of Paramount/Warner Bros., the latter of which owns Investigation Discovery. At first, Peacock had reservations about accepting the Wuornos gig — and not because of the whole serial killer thing. “Probably much like most people, as soon as you see ‘AI,’ you kind of go, ‘Hold on,’ you know? So it was really important that myself, my agent, we discussed it, and we got to grips with what it was that was being asked of me, and what was going to be the end result,” Peacock said. “I’m not redundant in any way, I haven’t been cloned. There isn’t an AI persona that’s being created — nothing like that’s happening,” she continued. “Once I’ve kind of got to, ‘Well, yeah, it’s basically kind of like CGI…and it’s still me.’ Then, yeah, I was comfortable with that.” One thing AI was definitely not was a shortcut. “Anyone who tells you that using AI speeds things up is wrong,” Dost said. “It slows things down by a lot — especially if you’re going to do it the right way.” It took three years to “ethically” use AI to make Unmasking a Monster , Dost said. He shared his ethical roadmap with us: Getting consent from the real people (homicide investigators, defense attorney, private investigator, Wuornos’ friend), as well as from the actors playing them. Not using the tech in cases where we could not get consent, like Mike Joyner, who died after giving his interview, or Tyria Moore, Aileen’s ex-girlfriend, who did not participate in the documentary. Ensuring authenticity throughout our scenes. Everything in the scenes comes directly from the transcripts, police records, and memories of our interview subjects. Nothing is invented for dramatic purposes. Being transparent about the process and the technology used. With interviews like these and behind-the-scenes videos to come, we want to be as transparent with our audience as we can about the process we used to visualize these new stories. Sarlanis said ID takes the “responsibility of every creative choice we make in crafting these complex stories very seriously.” “We knew that these tools, if used improperly, could and should warrant pushback. That’s why we took just as much time and care into developing the guidelines for how we would use the tech as we did in developing the capabilities of what the tech could do,” he continued. “Our focus was always on using these tools to empower the creativity of our filmmakers and in doing so we believe we’ve unlocked a way for the audience to experience this story in a uniquely authentic way.” (L to R) Sarah Paulson as Aileen Wuornos, Jessie Lee as Shelby in episode 406 of Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story. Courtesy of Netflix Dost and Peacock are not the only duo tackling Wuornos this month. About two weeks prior, Ryan Murphy’s Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story premiered on Netflix. Though Borden (played by Ella Beatty) is the star of the show, Wuornos (Sarah Paulson) is a substantial recurring character. The timing is “totally coincidental,” Dost said, but ultimately “a good thing.” Buzz about Monster can only help pique interest in Unmasking a Monster , and the two series don’t really play the same game. “Although they do scenes that are directly pulled from transcripts, they also imagine her as a Lizzie Borden admirer, which obviously she wasn’t,” Dost said. “Probably if she knew anything about the real Lizzie Borden, [Wuornos] would have hated Lizzie Borden. But it’s fiction, so that’s OK.” Between Paulson and Oscar winner Charlize Theron (for portraying Wuornos in 2003 film Monster ), Peacock is in good company — even if she didn’t previously know who Paulson is. (She’s since Googled her). “Everything Sarah Paulson does is amazing, and no, luckily Morag was not aware at the time that she would be up against Sarah Paulson,” Dost said, “because who would want that as a challenge?” Unmasking a Monster: Aileen Wuornos premieres tonight on ID and HBO Max. THR

title: As the CW Turns 20, the Once YA-Focused Network Takes a Look at the Road Ahead
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Sep 30, 2026 8:00am PT As the CW Turns 20, the Once YA-Focused Network Takes a Look at the Road Ahead By Michael Schneider Plus Icon Michael Schneider Executive Editor franklinavenue Latest Former CW Bosses Dawn Ostroff and Mark Pedowitz Look Back at the Network’s First 20 Years 3 minutes ago As the CW Turns 20, the Once YA-Focused Network Takes a Look at the Road Ahead 33 minutes ago ‘Jimmy Kimmel Live’ Kicks Off Broadcast’s Fall TV Premiere Week as No. 1 Show in Late Night (EXCLUSIVE) 24 hours ago See All The CW/Getty On a recent Saturday night, the CW found itself in an unusual position: Beating ABC and CBS in total viewers. Credit goes to their coverage of college football, as its Aug. 29 broadcast of a surprisingly competitive matchup between Florida State and New Mexico State averaged 2.1 million viewers, making it the most-watched sports broadcast in network history. Granted, the CW has only been in the sports business for three years. But it was a reminder that, as the network marks its 20th anniversary this month, the broadcast network is admittedly in quite a different place than it was even a few years ago. Related Stories Emmys Live Updates 2026 Emmys In Memoriam Excludes Chuck Norris, 'Buffy' Actor Nicholas Brendon and More And that’s by design: Under new owner Nexstar, which took over the CW in 2022, the network has undergone a rather dramatic transformation. While previous co-owners Warner Bros. and CBS utilized the CW as a place to program young adult dramas from its respective studios, Nexstar has aimed to broaden out the CW to focus on low-cost procedural drama acquisitions, repeatable unscripted fare and live sports that it feels better suits its stations’ needs. Popular on Variety Coincidentally, the final scripted holdover from the previous CW ownership, “All American,” wrapped its run with a series finale on Sept. 28. “I always greatly respected what Warner Bros. and CBS were doing with the CW and the brand they built,” says CW president Brad Schwartz . “But it was very clear when we took over that was probably not the type of business that could survive in the future. Our job was to create a network that the local stations can be successful with. “And that meant, how do we disrupt ourselves and move forward from this young adult scripted brand that was built over years and certainly was defined?” he continues. “Broadcast TV continues to be the greatest platform for bringing the most amount of people together simultaneously. And the product that is the best for doing that is sports. And so, if we were going to evolve the network, get the network to profitability, then moving into sports certainly became a very important strategy.” In building CW Sports, the network started with LIV Golf and then brought in Atlantic Coast Conference college football (joined later by deals with the Mountain West and Pac-12 conferences). The CW also has Professional Bowlers Assn. coverage, AVP beach volleyball and has signed a seven-year deal with NASCAR to air its O’Reilly Auto Parts Series, which consists of 33 races annually. According to NASCAR chief media and revenue officer exec vice president Brian Herbst, the O’Reilly series saw a 6% increase in viewership this year on the CW, on top of a 9% bump the previous year. “Every meeting that we had with the CW/Nexstar folks, it seemed like they were going to be aggressive in building out their content and programming plan,” Herbst says. “And one of the anchor properties that they were betting on was NASCAR. We thought the distribution strategy was great in terms of a free-to-air broadcast network across all 120 million-plus TV homes, as well as a marketing strategy at the Nexstar local station group level … We’re super happy with the results for the first couple of years, and we expect continued growth out of it for the balance of the term.” Meanwhile, the CW reunited with the WWE (which was part of the network’s initial 2006 launch with “Smackdown”) in 2024 with “WWE NXT ,” which airs live on Tuesdays. “Brad and his team are always finding fresh, creative ways to engage our core audience and reach new fans, all while staying true to the NXT brand,” says Shawn Michaels, senior VP of talent development creative at WWE. Schwartz says all of that adds up to 700 hours of live sports this year, up from zero just a few years ago. “The old CW used to just program two hours a night, seven nights a week,” he says. “We’re going to do over 1,250 hours of programming this year. Nearly half of that is now live sports.” Nexstar networks president Sean Compton adds that the company has calibrated the CW’s focus “as a program provider for affiliates. Properties like NASCAR, college football, basketball and WWE [pull] significant numbers of viewers to our stations, and that audience flow strengthens the entire local brand of those stations. That’s the outcome that matters to us the most being a company that owns a lot of local TV stations.” On the unscripted front, the CW has invested in repeatable franchises like the cop docuseries “Police 24/7,” as well as game shows like “Scrabble” (hosted by Craig Ferguson) and “Trivial Pursuit” (hosted by LeVar Burton). All three of those shows have been given large episodic orders so that they can be sold into daytime syndication, including on Nexstar stations. “While the syndication market’s gotten very thin, we’ve built those shows for our primetime audiences while complementing the off-net need for our stations, whether it’s daytime or in fringe time slots,” Compton says. “They debuted this fall in syndication with 94% clearance across the U.S. It’s a theme that we’re less reliant on major studios.” As “All American” ends, the CW continues to focus on acquisitions — particularly from Canada — to fill its scripted needs. That includes “Law & Order Toronto: Criminal Intent,” from Lark Prods., Cameron Pictures, Universal Global TV and Citytv; “Wild Cards,” from Blink49 Studios, Front Street Pictures and Piller/Segan, commissioned for CBC; “Sullivan’s Crossing,” from Reel World Management, CTV and Fremantle; and next up, “Private Eyes West Coast,” from Lionsgate Canada, Piller/ Segan and commissioned for Corus Entertainment in Canada. Lionsgate Television Group chair Kevin Beggs notes that Schwartz did something similar at Pop TV, where he programmed Canadian import “Schitt’s Creek,” which went on to be a critical and awards hit. “They all kind of knew at the CW that they have to reshape the model, and we are happy to be a supplier of that model,” Beggs says. “It’s not for every show, but for a really smart, efficiently produced drama or game show, it makes all the sense in the world — if we can figure out how to budget it correctly and keep the quality at a high level, which is really one of Brad’s skills. That’s how you have a small-budgeted show like ‘Schitt’s Creek’ relative for what he was paying, garner multiple Emmys and become the ‘it’ show of the year. It’s the dream. Everyone says, ‘Well, I want that.’ That’s what he’s doing there, and we’re excited to be part of it.” The CW’s new crop of dramas runs a bit more procedural, and skews broader than the young adult fare that most viewers remember from the network’s first 20 years. But Schwartz notes that the legacy of the CW’s YA fare lives on elsewhere, such as Netflix’s “Wednesday” and Prime Video’s “Sterling Point,” “Off Campus” and “The Summer I Turned Pretty.” “Those all are shows that would be classic CW shows,” he says. “But it was just very clear if you were going to build this business forward and make it profitable, that you had to change it.” ‘Reacher’ Spinoff ‘Neagley’ Trailer Teases Creepy Cult at Center of Murder Mystery Richard Madden to Star in Hostage Thriller Series ‘Trauma’ for Prime Video UK, Paramount+ (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Bloodaxe’ Season 2 Adds Five to Cast ‘Rose Hill’ Amazon Series Adds Siobhan McGroarty, Sophia Reid-Gantzert, West Mulholland Marta Kauffman Sets Improvised Sitcom ‘DINKS’ at Amazon Starring June Diane Raphael, Paul Scheer (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Sterling Point’ Renewed for Season 2 at Amazon Loading comments...

title: Bradley Whitford on Reuniting With Aaron Sorkin on Broadway and Getting a Star on the Walk of Fame: ‘Feels Like a Time Machine’
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Sep 30, 2026 8:00am PT Bradley Whitford on Reuniting With Aaron Sorkin on Broadway and Getting a Star on the Walk of Fame: ‘Feels Like a Time Machine’ By Carole Horst Plus Icon Carole Horst Latest ‘Gilmore Girls’ Comes to Life as Winter Holiday Event on Warner Bros. Studio Tour Hollywood in December 1 day ago Netflix’s Animated Drama ‘In Waves’ Opens the American French Film Festival, TV Competition Set 6 days ago ‘Fast & Furious: Hollywood Drift’ Ride Opens to Thrill Fans at Universal Studios Hollywood 2 weeks ago See All Todd Wiliamson/Disney For Bradley Whitford , being back on Broadway in “A Few Good Men” and reuniting with writer Aaron Sorkin, feels like “a time machine.” When Whitford was cast in the original 1989 Broadway production of “A Few Good Men,” little did he know a friendship and creative collaboration would be born — one that most notably led to the long-running series “The West Wing.” “It was an extraordinary thing, and it’s where I met Aaron. ‘The West Wing’ never would have happened if that hadn’t happened. It’s where we became friends,” Whitford says on a phone call from his New York base, where he’s in rehearsals for the new production of the iconic play. It opens Oct. 8 at Lincoln Center Theater, just about one week after he receives a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame Sept. 30. “West Wing” co-stars Martin Sheen and Dule Hill are scheduled to speak at the ceremony. In the revival, Whitford tackles Col. Jessup, so memorably played by Jack Nicholson in the 1992 film — and even if you’ve never seen the play or film, you know the line that Nicholson yells at Kaffee (Tom Cruise in the film): “You can’t handle the truth!” Since he landed the role, he’s repeatedly been asked about how he’ll say the iconic line. “I woke up and my lovely wife was kind of gazing at me, and she was just like, ‘How are you going to say it? I heard you running lines last night.’ And I’m like, ‘I’m not gonna do it.’ My own wife. This is ridiculous,” he says with a laugh. “I don’t know how I’m gonna do it. I shouldn’t know how I’m gonna do it. She’s like, ‘Do it,’ and I did it, and she was not impressed.” Sorkin was just 26 and Whitford, 30, when they first met. “We were talking about how strange it is because Aaron is like an institution. I’m doing this play where, frankly, it’s much better to be the understudy who surprises you,” he says in a characteristically self-deprecating way. In the original production, he played both Lt. Ross and the understudy for the role of Lt. Kaffee. “It’s much better to be that than the guy with his name on the poster. I can tell you that.” Whitford jokes about not taking acting seriously — “I love acting, I’m just not sure I respect it,” he says — telling a story about how after an L.A. screening of “Get Out,” “people were blown away.” “All these people, like, blowing smoke up my ass, and I’m kind of believing it,” he says. “My kid turns to me and very casually says, ‘No offense, Dad. I’ve seen dogs be good in movies.’ Which is only devastating because it’s true.” But it’s his way of staying grounded. He allows himself this aphorism: “The best way to take the work seriously is to not take yourself seriously doing the work. There are two atmospheres on a set. One is, ‘I hope you don’t fuck this up,’ and the other is, ‘I can’t wait to see what you’re gonna do.’ And now that I am a white-haired senior citizen about to have the star on the Walk of Fame, I know the best way to get to the good work is for the atmosphere to be more like recess than like school.” The three-time Emmy winner’s resume is packed with memorable characters, from “The West Wing,” “Studio 60 on the Sunset Strip,” “The Handmaid’s Tale” and “Transparent” to “Get Out,” “tick… tick… BOOM!,” “Death by Lightning” and, most recently, “The Diplomat.” But that’s just a fraction of his career. And he hopes to do more comedies moving forward, pointing to a short directed by his wife, Amy Landecker, for Funny or Die called “Bradley Whitford: Emotional Stuntman.” “That may be my favorite part ever,” he says, and you believe him. He also loved the work he did with her — and loved working with her — on her 2025 feature debut, the comedy “For Worse.” As for his honor on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, he feels odd. “I always said, there’s no segues in show business. You feel like you’re starting out, and then suddenly you’re Wilford fucking Brimley,” he says with a wry laugh. He thought about his late parents when he first got the Walk of Fame news. “I wish they could be there because they would really get a kick out of that. They certainly didn’t push me into show business, but I have vivid memories of my father’s joy at a high school play, taking a picture. They would really get a kick out of it that I get to spend all eternity with Allison Janney and Lucille Ball, dodging dog doo.” The kid from Wisconsin got hooked on acting in grade school — “I will probably never be better than I was in seventh grade as Teddy in ‘Arsenic and Old Lace,’” he says. “It sounds really corny, but I was like, Oh, my God! When I play a sport, I have to turn off my brain and my heart. When I read a book, I have to turn off my body. When I play an instrument, I have to stand still. But this is everything,” he remembers. “I really had that moment in seventh grade. Like, holy fuck, I need my brain. I need my heart. I need to prepare. I need to let go. And I guess I still enjoy that.” Back to the present, Whitford is thrilled to be reuniting with Sorkin for “A Few Good Men,” and sees the urgent relevancy to today in this 37-year-old play he says is about obeying — and so much more. “It’s not only about obeying illegal orders, it’s about what I think is a really fundamental question going on in the world: What is the best way to survive? Is it through cooperation, or is it through dominance?” he says. “And I see the play as a kind of an argument about that.” Though it raises questions about how we use the law to solve problems and the men in charge of the military, Sorkin’s writing is still infused with hope. Whitford feels that Sorkin is radical in his own way: “It’s kind of radical not to be cynical.” The actor is outspoken about his progressive politics and works closely with many different organizations. “Something I’ve been saying for a long time is — pulling together what a bunch of people have said — despair is a luxury that my children can’t afford, that their future can’t afford, and action is the antidote,” says Whitford. “What I see as the sort of civic virus of this malignant narcissist who has somehow gotten himself elected again, we have to fight our way out of this. We can’t give in to it.” He continues, “I’m actually amazed because I do a lot of stuff with the Democratic Party in my home state of Wisconsin. My fear is always that young people — justifiably — are going to check out, get cynical about the political process and leave that process and sentence themselves to a gulag dictated by the business interests who do participate in the political process. And I haven’t seen that happen. And I’m actually optimistic about how things are going to change politically, but boy, I didn’t see this coming.” He’s also very aware that some want celebrities to shut up about politics. “There’s nothing less democratic than telling people they should shut up. I try not to censor myself. I always feel like I should be doing more,” he says. “Uninformed celebrities spouting their idiotic political views start with the guy in the Oval Office.” Related Stories Never Mind the IP, Here's How Original Ideas Dominated This Year's Emmy Races 'Widow’s Bay' Wins Most Emmys Ever for a Comedy Series in a Year, Breaking 'The Studio’s' Record ‘Reacher’ Renewed for Season 6 Ahead of Season 5 Premiere ‘House of David’ to End With Season 3 at Amazon, Wonder Project Marta Kauffman Sets Improvised Sitcom ‘DINKS’ at Amazon Starring June Diane Raphael, Paul Scheer (EXCLUSIVE) Penn Badgley to Lead ‘Everyone in My Family Has Killed Someone’ Series at Amazon ‘Sterling Point’ Renewed for Season 2 at Amazon Richard Madden to Star in Hostage Thriller Series ‘Trauma’ for Prime Video UK, Paramount+ (EXCLUSIVE) Loading comments...

title: Pete Davidson Grows Up: On Leaving ‘SNL,’ Famous Exes, the Joys of Fatherhood and Why He’s Keeping His Hillary Clinton Tattoo
full_text: Continue to Variety SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Mary Ellen Matthews for Variety Say the name “ Pete Davidson ” aloud, and it will conjure a certain image: a man strutting down the street in baggy pants, swarmed by paparazzi, clenching the hand of a screen beauty with a grin on his face. A man who’s dated everyone from Ariana Grande and Margaret Qualley to Kate Beckinsale and Kim Kardashian , who inspired the term “big dick energy” and the earworm “Thank U, Next.” “There should be a group for us,” Davidson jokes of guys like himself and Jake Gyllenhaal who’ve been the subject of breakup anthems. “It’s something that comes up once in a while. But I think Ariana’s fuckin’ cool and immensely talented and an awesome girl. We’re not texting or whatever, but we’re cool.” Related Stories Zendaya Debuts Pixie Cut and Channels '90s Glamour at the Emmys 'Charlie's Angels' Reunion, Zendaya and 'Buffy' Alums Sarah Michelle Gellar, David Boreanaz Among Confirmed Emmys Presenters Mary Ellen Matthews for Variety It’s easy to see why women are drawn to Davidson. In person, he’s imposingly rangy and muscular and shoots you straight — a working-class fella from Staten Island, unlike those posh theater kids running around Hollywood. He’s also possessed of a wounded, underdog quality that invites warmth. You want him to be OK. Davidson’s lothario image has come to overshadow his obvious talent: In 2014, at the age of 20, he became one of the youngest “Saturday Night Live” cast members ever, regaling audiences with his direct-to-camera monologues about his mental health and the travails of living at home with his mom in Staten Island. By 26, he was starring in his own Judd Apatow-helmed biopic, “The King of Staten Island,” which was supposed to be his “Trainwreck” moment, only to have its release derailed by COVID. In the years since, he’s performed stand-up to sold-out theaters alongside pals Jon Stewart and John Mulaney; popped up in films like “Fast X” and “Dumb Money”; created and starred in “Bupkis,” a critically acclaimed TV series based on his life; dated a Kardashian; hosted his own talk show on Netflix; and fathered a child. Now the 32-year-old is making his big return to the silver screen in November’s “How to Rob a Bank,” playing a wounded war veteran who turns to robbing banks to provide for his family. He took the assignment seriously, packing on 15 pounds of muscle for the role. “I got on all the peptides that everyone’s doing. They work ,” he says. Davidson took Sermorelin and BPC-157 while training around the clock and consuming loads of protein. “I just think it’s really important for people to know that that’s what I did. When someone says, ‘Whoa, you’re in tremendous shape!’ and an actor goes, ‘Yup! Just broccoli, rice and chicken!,’ it’s like, ‘No, dude, you have a fuckin’ vein going from your forehead to your thumb.’” “How to Rob a Bank” is his most dramatic role yet, and he steals every scene he’s in. So are people finally ready to take Davidson seriously? Directed by David Leitch (“Bullet Train”) and hitting theaters Nov. 13, “How to Rob a Bank” is a hyperkinetic action film that follows a group of 20-somethings (led by Nicholas Hoult) who’ve been screwed by the system and turn to bank robbery as payback, livestreaming their heists on social media in the hope of igniting a movement. Davidson plays Vince, Hoult’s second in command and a veteran of the war in Afghanistan whose lungs have been ravaged by exposure to burn pits. “What Pete is doing in this movie isn’t something he’s put on. It’s him ,” says Leitch. “Pete, in real life, is one of the warmest, most engaging people I’ve ever worked with. Disarming. People feel safe around him in about 10 seconds.” Knowing his days are numbered, Vince robs banks to provide for his wife and young child. The film’s most heartbreaking scene sees Davidson’s character singing to his daughter over the phone before a deadly shootout ensues, and the actor nails it. No wonder: Right before filming, Davidson discovered he and his then-partner, Elsie Hewitt, were expecting a daughter. “Once I got in the room [with the young actress], I got really choked up. It really fucked me up.” His voice begins to crack. “What happens to the character is adjacent to what happened to me with my dad” — a firefighter who died in the line of duty on 9/11, when Davidson was 7 — “and the age and all that. … I’m a comic first, so I never understood when actors would be like, ‘It was very painful.’ But it is . It was very tough, and the first time I felt like a real actor because I wasn’t just playing myself.” The first time Davidson played himself was supposed to be his splashy movie-star debut. He’d received plaudits for his turn in the Sundance dramedy “Big Time Adolescence,” but “The King of Staten Island” was an Apatow movie dropping at South by Southwest — or at least that was the plan. It was March 2020, and the festival was canceled due to COVID. With theaters around the country shuttered, the movie was released digitally that June. Mary Ellen Matthews for Variety Davidson’s first thought was “I hope the world is OK.” Then came the intrusive ones. “It definitely helped me believe my self-fulfilling prophecy that I am doomed,” he recalls. The film was a particularly personal one for Davidson. In a story based on his Staten Island upbringing, the comic plays Scott, a 24-year-old high school dropout grappling with the loss of his firefighter father, who died in a blaze when Scott was 7. Scott (named for Davidson’s father) suffers from Crohn’s disease, PTSD and depression — just like Davidson. “I wanted to make ‘The King of Staten Island’ because I was interested in exploring the sacrifice Pete’s father made for others and how it affected Pete and his family,” explains Apatow. “Pete has always been able to find comedy in the most challenging subject matter. He is fearless, never censors his truth and is always willing to show you everything.” Bill Burr, whom he tapped to play his mother’s boyfriend in the film, lauded Davidson’s leadership on set: “He was considerate about everybody else’s time. And as the star, he could’ve requested to be shot out of scenes, and instead, he chose to have his fellow actors wrapped before him. It was a level of maturity and consideration that you don’t see a lot in any business.” It was in the summer of 2023, after the release of “Bupkis,” an autobiographical series on Peacock starring Davidson as himself, that Davidson says he reached rock bottom. He was one year removed from “Saturday Night Live,” which had given him much-needed structure, with no projects on the horizon. “Playing yourself and constantly living in your own crap” had forced him to revisit a number of harrowing moments in his life, so he used drugs to numb the pain. “It was K. I was getting liquid and cooking it,” he says. “And I would do acid and shrooms and whippets and smoke weed all day and eat pills every day. It got scary because I didn’t feel high. I felt high when I wasn’t doing it, so I was like, this is a huge problem.” An emotional FaceTime call with his mother, Amy, convinced him to get clean. “She told me her biggest fear was waking up one day to see on the news that something bad had happened to me,” recalls Davidson. “I reached a point where I couldn’t do that to her anymore.” Davidson checked himself into rehab and, even though Peacock had renewed “Bupkis” for a second season, walked away from the show. He was tired of playing himself, tired of turning his trauma into content. He wanted more for his career. He wanted, more than anything, to be taken seriously. “I was part of the problem of what I hated the most, which was the invasiveness around my personal life. I was just lobbing it up and continuing the narrative,” admits Davidson. He’d gone to rehab plenty of times to placate other people, but never because he really wanted to get clean. “When I turned 30 and I was there, it was a real low point. Nothing much was going on with my career and I was like, ‘This fuckin’ sucks. I can’t do it anymore.’ And it can’t be for anyone or for a job. You really have to want it, and when you’re done, you’re done.” Mary Ellen Matthews for Variety He says he’s sober now, save around “four beers a year.” “I don’t fuck with drugs anymore. It’s been two or three years from doing really hard stuff and about a year or more from weed. Weirdly, the hardest thing to stop was weed,” he says. “And now it’s easy because I have a kid. Anytime there’s ever a thought, I look at my phone background and go, ‘Oh yeah, no.’” On top of kicking drugs, Davidson is in the process of getting most of his nearly 200 tattoos removed. “One, they were fuckin’ horrible,” he cracks. “Two, it was a business decision. I hated coming into the makeup trailer three hours early to spray-paint over horrible fuckin’ tattoos. And third, I was like, ‘I’m not this dude.’ I got these when I was in an immense amount of pain and I was trying to show people my pain.” Davidson has struggled with self-harm. “I used to cut, so some of [the tattoos] covered up the cuts,” he says. He will be keeping a few, though, including the one of Hillary Clinton in a power suit on his right leg: “She stays. That’s my dog. I love Hillary, man. She’s awesome and a good friend.” As I wait for our interview to begin, Davidson is pacing the hotel room. We are moments away from capturing the cover photo — the comedian standing tall and triumphant atop lower Manhattan — and he’s adorned in a striped tracksuit and big dark sunglasses, the latter a remedy for the concussion he suffered days earlier shooting the film “Tommy Karate.” But Davidson seems with it — or is doing a really good job of acting like it. His head isn’t the thing bothering him at the moment. It is Sept. 9, one day before “NYC Still Rising After 25 Years,” a comedy benefit for 9/11 charities at Madison Square Garden organized by Davidson and Stewart and featuring an all-star roster of stand-up comics. Two of Davidson’s pals have bailed at the last minute. He removes his sunglasses and turns to his team. “Why the fuck would they do that?” he says. They shrug their shoulders. Then his phone rings. It isn’t another comedian dropping out of the event, but his ex, Hewitt. He answers and sees their 9-month-old daughter, Scottie, staring back at him. “Hello, sweetie!” he exclaims, beaming from ear to ear. “ Beebeebooboo, ” he coos while taking their FaceTime session to a back room and closing the door behind him. One minute passes. Then two. Then three. A crowd has formed in the room — publicists, assistants, photo editors — waiting on Davidson. We are now running behind schedule. Will he ever emerge? Ten minutes later, the door swings open, and it is as though all his troubles have washed away. Mary Ellen Matthews for Variety “Scottie is my whole life,” Davidson says of his baby girl, who’s named after Davidson’s dad. “I was living or dying on this business and what I thought people thought of me. It was all validation and ‘If I do this, then I’ll do that.’ But as soon as I saw her for the first time, I was like, ‘Oh my God, none of this fuckin’ matters at all . It’s a job. If I get to do cool stuff, great; if not, cool, I get to be home more with my kid.’” This time of year is always tough for Davidson. The loss of his father at such a young age left him with severe PTSD and crippling bouts of depression, which he manages to this day. “It’s tough going to firehouses where a lot of the guys knew my dad. It’s just a lot,” he says. “I got kind of used to it, but this year is different because of my kid. And I’ll be my dad’s age [when he died] in two months. Now I just understand it a little differently.” He pauses. “I understand it more from my mom’s side. That would be like my daughter’s mom not having me around and having to do it alone. My mom did that and never fuckin’ complained once. I look at that like, ‘Holy shit. My mom is the best. How fuckin’ lucky am I?’” There is also “the peanut gallery,” as he calls them — the army of online haters who’ve spent years scolding him for telling the occasional 9/11 joke as a way to cope with his grief. “For a while it bothered me when I would get, ‘Oh, why is he talking about 9/11 and his dad and all this stuff?’ from weird people on the internet, like it was all I talked about. I’ve made maybe five jokes about it in my specials over a span of 16 years, and then every 9/11 I try and do a benefit to help out. So I have my blinders on and do whatever I feel is necessary to do.” I ask Davidson about a recent tale told by President Trump at a 9/11 anniversary event involving a pair of firefighters lifting him from the rubble near ground zero mere moments after the attacks. (Records and eyewitness accounts show he was miles away at Trump Tower.) “Nothing that guy says is surprising anymore,” Davidson laments. “It’s sad that it’s to the point where it’s so ridiculous that you’re like, ‘Yeah, whatever. ’ He’s the drunk uncle, but he has the keys to the nukes. That’s the problem. If he didn’t have those keys, you’d be like, ‘Oh, that’s just the silly drunk uncle. He’s old.’ That’s unfortunate that he said that, though, because that’s definitely not what happened.” As a teenager, Davidson would sit in the back of the bus and write jokes on his way to and from basketball games and try them on his teammates. They eventually goaded a 16-year-old Davidson to enter an open mic night called “Wacky Wednesdays” at The Looney Bin, a Staten Island comedy club tucked inside a bowling alley. “There were four people there, it went good enough, and I really loved it and got addicted to the laughs,” he remembers. “Growing up not having many friends and having a moment where you’re talking and everyone’s listening was very attractive to me.” His first TV performance came on the VH1 reality series “Mob Wives.” Set in Staten Island, the show followed a number of women whose husbands were jailed for mob-related activities. Davidson was 18 and working as a chauffeur in real life, driving a guy around Staten Island. “I had to drive him to a party, and something happened where there was a fight, and he ran back into the car with his suit ripped in half,” Davidson says laughing. “I drove the getaway car. That’s my first TV gig ever.” Then Davidson joined “ SNL .” He got the gig thanks in large part to Bill Hader, who acted with the young comedian in “Trainwreck.” “He was in one scene in the movie, and I thought he was funny, so I texted Lorne [Michaels] and sent him a video of Pete’s stand-up. He obviously loved it,” Hader recalls, adding, “He didn’t need much advice. He was self-possessed and eager to show his stuff.” Davidson says it took him a while to settle into “SNL”: “I wanted to leave after my first year and asked Lorne to leave every year. I was like, ‘I don’t fuckin’ work in this! And I just tell my stand-up on ‘Update’ and then burn it and can’t do it on the road, and I just want to do stand-up,’ and he’d always be like, ‘You’ll figure it out after four years.’ And he was right.” Davidson found his footing with the character Chad, a monosyllabic stoner who navigates intense situations with apathy, and the memorable Please Don’t Destroy sketch “Three Sad Virgins” with Taylor Swift. He decided to walk away from “SNL” in 2022. “After eight years, it was just time. I just happened to be 28 when I left, so it was a little weird, but Lorne was cool with it. I love Lorne. He’s my Yoda. I love him very much, and I’m grateful that we’re still pals.” It was on “SNL” that Davidson met Kim Kardashian. The two shared a kiss as Aladdin and Jasmine in an October 2021 sketch and began dating shortly thereafter. Davidson was thrust into a reality-TV world of prying paparazzi and untold media scrutiny. “I’m one of the survivors — the few and the proud. We’re like the Marines,” he jokes of men who’ve dated Kardashians. “Look, man, that’s a really tough atmosphere if you’re not game. One of the things I love about Kim and that whole family is they’re like, ‘This is what we do.’ I found that very attractive and mature. “And I was never subjected to anything I didn’t want to be a part of. She was super respectful of all of it, but the craze of that lifestyle — being followed everywhere, having security and looking over your shoulder — for a guy with mental stuff, and at the time drug problems, was a little too much for me. But we’re cool, and I have a lot of love for her, and I knew what I was getting into.” Mary Ellen Matthews for Variety The one thing he couldn’t predict was the wrath of her ex, Kanye West . Kardashian was still in the process of divorcing West when she began dating Davidson, and the rapper took it upon himself to make Davidson’s life a living hell, posting threats on Instagram and, in the music video for his song “Eazy,” depicting a Claymation Davidson getting kidnapped and beheaded. “What tripped me out is I was super open about mental stuff — everyone knows this about me — and it’s like he was [saying], ‘Kill yourself.’ And he did push me.” As for whether Davidson, who’s half-Jewish, thinks he’s the reason why West started going on antisemitic rants, he chuckles. “What people don’t understand about that dude — and I’m not one-one-millionth as talented or influential or powerful as that dude, but I have dealt with a fraction of what he’s had to deal with public-wise — is that’ll do it. He’s also lost a parent and has mental stuff, and I don’t know how he deals with it or who he has around him. Probably a lot of people who want to be his friend. I’ve had that. When people are so far up your ass and constantly pushing and provoking you and not showing you love, you want to burn it all. I think it got to a certain point where he was like, ‘Leave me the fuck alone. I’m just going to say crazy shit.’ There’s zero way he really feels like that.” Davidson jokes he did Kardashian a service by absorbing West’s attacks. “I like to think I got that one out of the way for her because whoever that guy was going to be was gonna get it,” he remarks. “I cleared the path for her to get back into the dating pool.” As someone who deals with an immense amount of scrutiny regarding his own appearance, Davidson is pained to see the vitriol another ex, Grande, has been subjected to of late. “I don’t like it at all. It’s not cool. She’s a really strong person — I’ve witnessed it — and I don’t understand it. She knows how to handle this stuff though. She’s been around. So she’ll be OK, but I think it’s fucked up.” The most frustrating thing for Davidson when it comes to his dating life — and the media’s fixation on it — is the amount he feels it’s detracted from his career, reinforcing the idea that he’s unserious, girl-crazy tabloid fodder. “It’s been over a decade. My work and my relevance is super overlooked, and it’s confusing to me,” he declares, suddenly working himself into a lather. We’ve struck a nerve. “I’m still only 32, but I have really crazy credits: nearly a decade at ‘SNL’; I hosted a year after I left; I worked with Gillespie and Gunn and Liman and Leitch and Judd and Edie and Pesci.” (Craig Gillespie, James Gunn and Doug Liman directed Davidson in, respectively, “Dumb Money,” “The Suicide Squad” and the forthcoming “Bitcoin.”) Davidson’s voice is getting louder as he runs through his self-defense. “What the fuck do I have to do? And look, I get it — I’ve dated a lot of people. But so has everyone else! Everyone is fucking everyone in this business! Everyone! And for some reason it’s zeroed in on me, and I can’t feel sorry for myself because I put myself in those situations, but everyone else is doing it. I was in my 20s. Am I not supposed to fuck around and do drugs and have fun and be in Hollywood like everybody else? Sorry, everyone!” If “How to Rob a Bank” is evidence that Davidson can nail a dramatic role, then “Tommy Karate” is the film he believes will really change people’s perception of him as an actor. Directed by Justin Chon from a screenplay Davidson wrote during his rehab stint in 2023, the film centers on Thomas Pitera, aka “Tommy Karate” — a real-life hit man for New York’s Bonanno crime family who is suspected of murdering 60 people. Pitera is tracked down by DEA agent Jim Hunt (Paul Walter Hauser), with Camila Mendes, Simon Rex and Gina Gershon joining in on the fun. When Davidson sent the script around town, it received plenty of positive feedback, except for the idea that Davidson would portray Pitera. “They were like, ‘Pete Davidson? Fuck him, ’” he recalls. “And I was like, ‘OK, I’m pretty used to it.’” He spent years shopping it around and considered letting someone else take on the role until a Zoom chat with Sylvester Stallone convinced him otherwise. Davidson contacted Stallone because he was trying to remake his favorite Stallone movie, the 1981 cop thriller “Nighthawks.” “He said something that really fucked me up,” Davidson recalls. “He goes, ‘I’ve seen some of your work. I think you could be a really good actor, but no one’s ever going to write a part for you that’s good. You have to write it yourself, and you have to take it.’ I was like, ‘Rocky is telling me to make “Rocky.”‘” Pete Davidson in “How to Rob a Bank” Megan Schoenbachler Davidson just wrapped principal photography on “Tommy Karate,” but photos from the Atlanta set depicting him in a clumsy wig and icy blue contacts leaked online, leading to more sniping at his expense. “I wish my fuckin’ wig was set, and I wasn’t eating in my photos. I promise you it doesn’t look like that in the movie,” he says. “If ‘Tommy Karate’ is not my coming-out party, then I have zero pulse on this business at all. I think people are going to be really surprised and be like, ‘What the fuck.’ And I’m not online, but I see what people are saying. It’s all negative. It’s so in the toilet and the bar is so low that it makes me even more excited. I hope more people trash it before it comes out because they really have no fuckin’ idea what we did. We’re really proud of it.” “Tommy Karate” is expected to hit theaters in fall 2027 after making the festival rounds. Davidson also has wrapped “Wizards!,” a stoner comedy from David Michôd, and “Bitcoin,” a thriller about the cryptocurrency and its mysterious founder, Satoshi Nakamoto. He’s happy to be back in New York City, the place he’s called home his whole life. “You can have the absolute worst day of your life in public here, and nobody blinks. Everyone minds their own business because they’ve got somewhere to be,” he says. But he’s mostly excited about spending time with Scottie, pushing her stroller around their Brooklyn neighborhood and trying to make her laugh. “It’s a lot of trial and error and a lot of bombing. If you think I bombed on ‘SNL,’ you should see me with my fuckin’ daughter.” Whenever he talks about Scottie, Davidson lights up. He is adamant that he’s doing a lot better, and Scottie is the reason. “It’s filling a lot of emptiness. If you think the internet’s sick of Pete Davidson, I’m sick of it. I’m exhausted from being me all the time . That it’s all about her first is the best gift ever. It’s an indescribable feeling.” He smiles. “It’s the best, man. title: San Quentin Film Festival 2026 Lineup Revealed (Exclusive)
full_text: × Skip to main content By Tony Maglio Plus Icon Tony Maglio View All September 30, 2026 7:57am Prisoners at dinner, Michigan City, Ind. 1907 Library of Congress The Hollywood Reporter can exclusively reveal the official selections for the 2026 San Quentin Film Festival (SQFF26). The third-annual installment is set for Oct. 22–23 at the San Quentin Rehabilitation Center in Marin County, Calif. — SQFF26 remains the only film festival held inside of a U.S. prison. It’s there for good reason: SQFF honors the creative work of current and former incarcerated filmmakers, “spotlighting stories of resilience, redemption and artistic expression from behind the walls, in competition with filmmakers from across the country and around the world,” per the festival. Related Stories Movies Oscar-Nominated Documentary 'Cutting Through Rocks' Among Athena Film Festival Award Winners (Exclusive) Movies A New York Startup Just Threw a Splashy Event to Hail the Future of AI Movies “When this festival began, we dreamed of bringing films from different prisons and countries into conversation with one another, while giving formerly incarcerated artists a place for their voices to be heard,” said Cori Thomas, SQFF co-founder and artistic director. “Filmmakers who explore incarceration through their work are part of that conversation, too. I’m thrilled that artists from Cameroon, South Africa, Italy, Spain, and Germany are joining American filmmakers this year. And it is especially meaningful to present special selections from five prisons, including San Quentin. Together, these films create the vibrant chorus of voices we hoped this festival would become.” The 2026 program has a preview night, Wednesday, Oct. 21, when the first hour of Lynn Novick’s upcoming four-part PBS documentary series Crime and Punishment in America , which features one hell of an impressive voice cast, will screen for an audience of San Quentin residents (we would formerly call them inmates). Directed by Novick ( The Vietnam War , Hemingway , College Behind Bars , The U.S. and the Holocaust ) and executive produced by Ken Burns and Sam Pollard, the eight-hour series “explores the history of criminal justice in America, from the pre-colonial period through 21st-century mass incarceration, examining how the intertwined forces of law, power, race and class have shaped and reflected the American experience across four centuries,” according to its synopsis. A panel discussion with Novick; SQFF co-founder and series consulting producer Rahsaan Thomas, and “survivor advocates” Annie and Jess Nichol will follow. The conversation will be moderated by Kevin D. Sawyer, former editor-in-chief of San Quentin News and recipient of the SQFF24 Best Pitch Award for his documentary project, The History of Prison Journalism . “The San Quentin Film Festival is an incredible event doing vital, transformative work, bridging communities through the profound power of storytelling and film,” Novick said in a statement. “We feel deeply honored and lucky to share our series in such a unique and important space.” Narrated by Keith David, Crime and Punishment in America features voice performances by Samuel L. Jackson, Laura Linney, Bobby Cannavale, Matthew Rhys, Michael Stuhlbarg, David Hyde Pierce and BD Wong. The series is produced by Lucas Frank, Vanessa González-Block, Lynn Novick and Prisca Pointdujour. It will air over four consecutive nights on PBS beginning Nov. 16, 2026, and will stream on all PBS digital platforms for four weeks. Jail Time Records. Courtesy of Jail Time Records The 2026 San Quentin Film Festival received 75 submissions for its 2026 competition. The Short Film categories, open exclusively to currently and formerly incarcerated filmmakers, are judged by SQFF’s Industry Jury, the Feature category is evaluated by an Inside Jury composed of San Quentin residents, and the Long Short category is judged by an Inside Jury of residents at Central California Women’s Facility. (“Long Short” is new this year and is comprised of films running up to 40 minutes — the in-betweeners.) The fest’s pitch competition received an additional 68 submissions from incarcerated writers at 20 facilities across America (and one in Panama — the first ever from outside the U.S.). SQFF’s Industry Jury selects the winners. Nearly 400 people will attend the two-day festival — half entertainment industry professionals and the other half San Quentin Rehabilitation Center residents. Those who cannot attend will be able to screen the official selections from Oct. 26 to Nov. 8 via screening passes available for sale. Incarcerated people in California will be able to watch the films through the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation (CDCR) institutional channel. Courtesy of Netflix Logo text A woeful update for Wednesday fans wondering when they’ll get a third season. The good news is the third season of the Netflix supernatural hit has just wrapped production. The bad news is that still means a long wait for the new episodes given the show’s extensive post-production effects work. There was a three-year gap between season one (2022) and season two (2025).
