title: John Grover, Film Editor on Six James Bond Movies, Dies at 87
full_text: Skip to main content By Rhett Bartlett Plus Icon Rhett Bartlett dialmformovies Follow Sign Up View All September 30, 2026 7:07am John Grover Courtesy of British Film Editors John Grover, the British film editor who helped assemble a half-dozen James Bond movies and spent six long months breathing heavily at the behest of Stanley Kubrick for 2001: A Space Odyssey , has died. He was 87. Grover, a longtime vice chairman of the British Film Editors who received their Lifetime Achievement Award in April, died Monday at his home in Buckinghamshire, England, following a short illness, his son, Tim, told The Hollywood Reporter . Grover served as the film editor on the 007 films For Your Eyes Only (1981), The Living Daylights (1987) and Licence to Kill (1989) and also helped put together The Spy Who Loved Me (1977), Moonraker (1979) and Octopussy (1983) . Related Stories Movies Two-Time Oscar Winner and 'Atonement' Writer Christopher Hampton to Lead Tallinn Film Fest Jury Business From 'F1' to 'Slow Horses' to 'Call My Agent!': Mediawan Executives Take Madrid Spotlight In all, he did six films starring Bond star Roger Moore , including The Wild Geese (1978 ) and The Sea Wolves (1980), and also cut The Final Option (1982), Tobe Hooper’s Lifeforce (1985), the 1984 NBC miniseries The First Olympics and what he said was his favorite film, Jim Henson’s classic Labyrinth (1986). Early in his career, Grover worked as an uncredited assistant editor for Robert Wise on The Haunting (1963), for David Lean on Doctor Zhivago (1965), for John Frankenheimer on Grand Prix (1966), for Kubrick on 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968) and for Herbert Ross on Goodbye, Mr. Chips (1969). During a 2016 editing conference, Grover talked about his awful experience dealing with Kubrick, the manically perfectionist director of 2001 . “I spent six months of my life with that idiot,” Grover said. “Although he was a supposedly good filmmaker, he was mad. He’d kill the artist by [saying] keep going again and again and again.” “I think [ 2001 is] a load of rubbish, it’s the most boring, long, stretched out [film]. I mean, OK, it was very clever [with its] use of original music, which we had to get back from Germany, ‘The Blue Danube’ and all that. It’s very ahead of its time; what actually we were doing in imagination actually happened, and the space stations are now up there.” In his 2018 book Space Odyssey: Stanley Kubrick, Arthur C. Clarke, and the Making of a Masterpiece, Michael Benson wrote that Grover accompanied editorial assistant David de Wilde to record Kubrick — battling a head cold — breathing heavily. The audio was then used to accentuate tense scenes featuring astronauts Dave Bowman (Keir Dullea) and Frank Poole (Gary Lockwood). “With Grover’s help, they ran a microphone from the soundboard in the theater and positioned it next to Kubrick’s face, after which he lowered the helmet onto his shoulders,” Benson explained. But Grover claimed that it was he, not the director, who did the laborious inhaling and exhaling that’s heard in the movie. “All I did was breathing for six months,” he said. “[Kubrick] wanted it done with the helmet … He’d sit right at the front … with a notebook, and you’d run the sequence and he’d be writing and he’d come back and say, ‘OK, John, very good, do it again.’ You had to watch [the film] pretending you were doing exercises and straining and moving things.” A spokesperson for the British editors guild said “both Stanley K. and John Grover were recorded for the ‘heavy breathing’ — and it is thought that the recording of John was the one used for the film.” What is known for certain is that the breaths were recorded simultaneously on two rolls of 35mm film, in 10-minute takes, so that Grover could more easily cut between them when removing ambient noise. A decade later, Grover was assembly editor on another space-set adventure, Lewis Gilbert’s Moonraker. Working alongside editor John Glen, they cobbled together the final cut of that Bond movie from 800,000 feet of film. It took 10 months — until the day before the premiere — to be completed. On The Spy Who Loved Me , Grover was tasked with editing the iconic pre-credit sequence that culminates with Moore skiing and then parachuting off a cliff. With Glen stationed with the second-unit team in Switzerland and then in Baffin Island, Canada, Grover waited back in the studio for the rushes. “I was in the cutting room preparing, waiting for film and it didn’t come in, because they couldn’t shoot it,” he said. After a 10-day wait because of atrocious weather, the crew was able to film the spectacular jump during a 15-minute break in the harsh conditions. In his final edit, Grover snuck in a music box he was given on the set of Doctor Zhivago that played “Lara’s Theme” and was used by Anya Amasova (Barbara Bach) in The Spy Who Loved Me . Composer Maurice Jarre received royalties for the brief use of his leitmotif. Born on Oct. 24, 1938, in Barnet, Middlesex, England, Grover enlisted in National Service as a teenager. Upon his return, he started as a numbering boy at MGM Studios, where his uncle was supervising editor, earning 6 pounds 10 shillings a week. Grover said he enjoyed working with Lean, who was opinionated yet open to collaboration. “He’d say, ‘Get everybody in here, let’s have a look at this, what do you think?’ ” he noted. “He’d listen to you, provided you had an answer.” He recalled that Zhivago’s 70mm Los Angeles premiere was interrupted by a loud bang from the projection booth at the first change-over reel. A gear box had exploded, causing the screen to plunge into darkness for eight minutes. A larger disaster unfolded during the postproduction of The Living Daylights when a work print containing dialogue sequences was leaked and circulated on VHS. Grover, who co-edited Timothy Dalton’s 007 debut with Peter Davies, was called into the office of producer Albert Broccoli and associate producer Tom Pevsner. “That was really frightening,” he remembered in 2018. “Of course we were the No. 1 suspects; we were in the cutting rooms, we were the only one who had access to it.” But Grover revealed that whenever parts of the film were sent away, he would mark a single frame with an identifiable symbol and document who it was sent to. “We found out it had been copied and duplicated in New York by the trailer company, which immediately went bust,” he said. In addition to his son, survivors include his wife of 62 years, Jenny; daughter Camilla; five grandchildren; and two great-grandchildren. After his retirement, Grover recalled the formula that Bond producers and directors used that helped make the franchise an everlasting success. “Bad language was unacceptable, but some violence and sexual innuendo was OK,” he said. “Family entertainment was their motto. Grandparents could always take their grandchildren to see the films to enjoy them together.” Moore was his favorite Bond actor, and his favorite 007 scene was the car and circus-train chase on railway tracks in Octopussy , he said. “For God’s sake, we got on those pictures, and for nine months I basically would never go home,” he added. “So you had to have a good family behind you.” THR

title: ‘Digger’ Ad Fires Back at Critics With Tom Cruise Character Declaring “F**k Those People”
full_text: × Skip to main content By James Hibberd Plus Icon James Hibberd Writer-at-Large JamesHibberd Follow Sign Up View All September 30, 2026 7:04am Ross Hatt with Tom Cruise (right) in 'Digger,' a Warner Bros. Pictures release. Courtesy Warner Bros. Pictures Don’t listen to those hoity-toity critics. Go see Digger and make up your own mind . That’s the gist behind Warner Bros.’ online ad for the new Alejandro G. Iñárritu film, which is receiving some scathing reviews (and, to be fair, many rather positive ones, as well). “Decide for yourself,” declares the text introducing the ad (below). The ad then kicks off with a critic quote saying Digger “is an ambitious film sure to polarize audiences,” before Tom Cruise ’s titular character exclaims, “You know what? Fuck those people!” Related Stories Movies Tom Cruise Slams AI, Defends $125M 'Digger' as Reviews Divide Critics: "People Want Real Things" Movies Tom Cruise 'Digger' Reviews Are Brutally Split: From "Insufferable" to "Terrific" Other contrasting critic quote messages flash across the screen, juxtaposing the words “Unpleasant” and “Masterpiece,” and then, “Baffling” and “Brilliant,” and “Insufferable” and “Magnificent.” The ad ends with Cruise’s character saying, “Never be afraid to tell the truth — whatever that is.” It’s a pretty bold ad for a rather bold film, essentially telling moviegoers: “Some people really dislike this movie, so go buy a ticket to find out why and, hey, maybe you’ll agree — or not.” The studio must have had some idea that the film was going to get pilloried in some corners as the ad went live even before the review embargo broke Tuesday. The $125 million production stars a nearly unrecognizable Cruise playing an oblivious oil tycoon whose drilling in Greenland dislodges an ice shelf from a glacier that’s going to cause a global disaster. He must race to prove that he’s humanity’s savior before the ecological accident wreaks havoc on the planet. At least, that’s the film’s ostensible setup. Digger contains a twist upending its narrative that’s complicated the reviews and discussion as critics have been tiptoeing around describing the film’s actual meta storyline. Decide for yourself. DIGGER – in theaters and IMAX FRIDAY. Tickets on sale now. https://t.co/Z1IpSpFnXd pic.twitter.com/e5ID4WUxbL — Warner Bros. (@warnerbros) September 29, 2026 Some critics have praised the film as a bold and timely story with incredible production design and features Cruise clearly giving the role everything he’s got in a bombastic performance. But others have slammed the effort as a pretentious and obnoxious slog. The Hollywood Reporter ‘s David Rooney wrote that Digger is “a climate crisis satire so smug and bombastic it makes Adam McKay’s Don’t Look Up seem almost innocuous. Digger is basically what happens when you put two outsize egos together with nobody holding the reins to keep their most self-indulgent impulses in check … so meta that you watch in excruciating weariness as [the film] disappears up its own ass and then realize to your dismay that there’s another eardrum-shattering hour left to endure … It’s difficult to imagine mainstream audiences ever wanting to be a part of this bludgeoning ordeal.” While reviews are still coming in, so far Digger has a 53 percent positive rating on Rotten Tomatoes across 113 reviews, a split that almost perfectly reflects the polarized response to the film. Digger opens in theaters Friday, Oct. 2. THR

title: Why ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Isn’t Live on the West Coast
full_text: Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All September 30, 2026 6:53am 'Dancing With the Stars' season 35. Disney/Christopher Willard Logo text Every Dancing With the Stars episode used to begin with the iconic introduction: “Live from Hollywood, it’s Dancing With the Stars !” But for those tuning in from the West Coast, the show isn’t live at all. Season 35 of Dancing With the Stars airs Tuesdays at 8 p.m. for both coasts, simulcasting across ABC and Disney+, streaming the next day on Hulu. New episodes begin filming in Los Angeles at 5 p.m. PT, airing immediately for the East Coast audience at 8 p.m. ET, but not until 8 p.m. PT. for the West Coast audience. Related Stories TV 'Dancing With the Stars' Sets Super Bowl Night TV 'Dancing With the Stars' Caps Yacht Rock Night With a Shock Elimination: See the Scores, Who Went Home The discrepancy in air time is a pain point West Coast viewers who are easily spoiled on social media about how couples fared. Voting also only takes place during the live taping, meaning West Coasters have to “blindly vote” for their favorite celebrities and remember to send in their votes in from roughly 5 p.m. to 6:45 p.m. if they want to be counted. Dancing With the Stars has historically utilized this format for airing the show, but that hasn’t made viewers any less frustrated. Season 31 was exclusively streamed on Disney+, and began at 5 p.m. PT; the show returned to ABC for season 32, though, and has since retained its method of airing at 8 p.m. for both coasts. “I’m angry and sad that The West Coast cannot watch the premiere live!” reads the title of a Reddit thread from 2023 when Dancing With the Stars shifted back to ABC for its 32nd season. The same user wrote, “Please help me understand why The West Coast cannot watch the premiere or future episodes of Dancing With The Stars live on Disney plus? It makes no sense and I’m furious! It almost makes me want to boycott the show.” A recent Reddit thread left another user with the same confusion about the show’s air time: “The show does not air live on the west coast. Not entirely sure WHY, but it doesn’t air live. So the show has happened, you have to vote blind, and you’ll get to watch at it at your appointed time.” The reason Dancing With the Stars doesn’t air live for its West Coast audience stems back to local news and the coveted primetime programming slots. Evening news is a major primetime program, and airing hours belong to differing identities, meaning ABC can’t just shift Dancing With the Stars into that 5 p.m. PT slot. One outlier to this more-often-than-not rule is Saturday Night Live ; the late-night show airs at 8:30 p.m. PT/11:30 pm ET on NBC, also simulcasting on Peacock. However, since it airs somewhat later for the West Coast and on Saturday nights, local news won’t be disrupted by showing new episodes. The Hollywood Reporter recently spoke with showrunner Conrad Green for a DWTS season 34 finale piece , and when THR asked Green why Dancing With the Stars doesn’t air or stream live for the West Coast, he clarified that the question is moreso “a discussion with the affiliates who show the show across the network [ABC] all over the country. “It’s a big issue for them is if everyone starts watching the show at 5 p.m. when it airs. If you’re in L.A. and you watch at 5 p.m. when it airs [at 8 p.m.] on the East Coast, then it’s going to massively affect the people who will watch the show when it comes over to these different territories and those markets,” he said. “The affiliates are hugely important in the bigger picture for the overall economic structure of the show and for the history of ABC and all of those things.” Green said he understands the frustration from West Coast viewers, “but the good thing is, you can still vote. You’re just basically voting blind. But if you love someone, you can set your alarm for five o’clock and vote 10 times for them on both methods and make sure your voice is heard. It just requires a bit of forward planning ( laughs ).” THR also asked if Green knew why every Dancing With the Stars season wasn’t available to stream on Disney+. (As of Sept. 2026, only seasons 31-35 are available to watch.) “I haven’t had that conversation with Disney+, but the rights to restream the show are expensive; the licensing terms for the music we use on the show and all of those kind of things are pretty significant,” he said. “So I guess there’s a calculation to be made about how much interest is there in previous seasons versus the cost of having them on a platform.” West Coast viewers who aren’t able to tune in live can keep up with Dancing With the Stars by following along with THR ’s weekly live recaps . Or wait until 8 p.m. PT to watch — but make sure you get your votes in by 6:45 p.m. PT. THR reached out to ABC for comment, but did not hear back by the time of publication. THR

title: Condé Nast CEO Roger Lynch Jumps To Top Job At Mattel, Succeeding Ynon Kreiz
full_text: Skip to main content By Dade Hayes Dade Hayes Business Editor @dadehayes More Stories By Dade Disney Hit By Layoffs, A Couple Hundred Workers Cut Broadcast To Hit A Double, Peacock Going Deep In NBC Sports Coverage Of MLB Wild Card Playoffs Paramount To Move Its Class B Shares From Nasdaq To New York Stock Exchange In Early October View All September 30, 2026 6:45am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Roger Lynch, left, is stepping down as CEO of Condé Nast to take the top exec job at Mattel, replacing Ynon Kreiz. Getty Images/Teri Weber Condé Nast CEO Roger Lynch has stepped down in order to take the top job at Mattel . Ynon Kreiz , who steered the toymaker through its Barbie movie breakthrough, is poised to take “a senior leadership position at another public company,” an announcement by Mattel said Wednesday. Lynch, whose appointment as CEO takes effect on November 2, will become chairman on October 2. He has been a member of Mattel’s board of directors since 2018. Lynch took over Condé Nast as CEO in 2019, helping the publishing giant navigate declines in print readership and advertising along with Covid. He will remain on the company’s board of directors. Related Stories Executives Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch's Total Pay Declines To $31M In Fiscal 2026 From $33M In Prior Year News Mattel Studios Boss Says "We All Want To See The 'Barbie' Sequel" But Timing Remains Unclear The move follows what Mattel described as a “comprehensive succession planning process” after Kreiz spent eight years running the company. Board member Judy Olian, who led the succession process, called Lynch “a visionary leader with a track record of growing global companies at the forefront of changing industry and consumer trends.” Watch on Deadline Before leading the parent company of Vogue and the New Yorker, Lynch was CEO of music streamer Pandora and the founding chief exec of Sling TV, the streaming pay-TV provider launched a decade ago by Dish Network. Along with the inherent complexities of running a media company born in the 20th century as it reckoned with the consumer habits and tech innovations of the 21st, artificial intelligence was a major challenge. Condé Nast, like other publishers, has seen its web traffic decline as AI chatbots aggregate information that readers would previously have sought out on media platforms. Mike Perlis, lead independent board member for Condé Nast who has previously run media companies Forbes and Ziff Davis, will become interim CEO while a search for a permanent top exec is conducted. Kreiz, who previously had CEO stints at Endemol Group, Fox Kids Europe and Maker Studios before its acquisition by Disney, turned Mattel toward Hollywood during his eight years at the helm. The main fruit of that effort was Barbie , which became a global phenomenon in 2023, grossing $1.4 billion and netting multiple Oscar nominations. Efforts to make a Barbie sequel have run aground on budget issues, however. A Hot Wheels movie project is in development, but the flow of entertainment adaptations has been erratic. Mattel stock has fallen 31% over the past five years. “It has been a privilege to lead Mattel, with a global team dedicated to its mission and purpose, and I am proud of all we have achieved together,” Kreiz said in a statement. “I have every confidence the company will continue to thrive under Roger’s leadership.” Lynch said during his time on Mattel’s board, he came to admire its “brands, its talented people, and unique culture. I am especially grateful to Ynon for his many years of outstanding leadership and service to the company.” CA Gov Candidate Steve Hilton On Federal Tax Credits, ParaBros Merger & More ‘Ted Lasso’ Shocker: Actor Reflects On Death Of OG Character BBC Studios Scripted Boss Jamie Hall On Talent Deal Strategy Review & Red Carpet Premiere Photos With Anne Hathaway, Dakota Johnson Read More About: 1 Comments

title: Ahead Of Tonight’s CNN Gubernatorial Debate, Steve Hilton On No Federal Tax Credits This Year, ParaBros Politics, L.A.’s Next Mayor & California’s Spirit
full_text: Skip to main content By Dominic Patten Dominic Patten Executive Editor, Legal, Labor & Politics @DeadlineDominic More Stories By Dominic Trump “Very Close” To Unveiling AI Czar, Praises Techlords Inking “Morally Binding” Self-Regulation Pact As Tech Rebranded Blue State AGs Side With Paramount, Scolding Sen. Cory Booker Over Settlement Opposition: “A Negotiated Agreement …Includes Compromises On Behalf Of All Of The Parties Involved” ParaBros Foes Urge Court To Reject Settlement In Midnight Filings: “This Merger Lessens Competition” View All September 30, 2026 6:45am Add us as a Google Preferred Source David Ellison, Donald Trump and Steve Hilton Getty Images “People actually want to be in California and in L.A. particularly, and so I think we don’t have to go crazy,” says gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton on the need for greater film and TV tax incentives in the Golden State and from the federal government. Related Stories News CNN, MS NOW And Politico Warn That Trump Will “Reinstitute A Complete Ban” Without Judge’s Injunction: “An Injury On All News Media” News Film Execs Ponder Federal Film Tax Credit Impact, Timeline & Potential Price Rises — Zurich Summit “We just have to match the best, and we have to be as good as the best,” the Brit-born ex-host of Fox News’ The Next Revolution adds of the lucrative jurisdictions of the UK, Canada and Europe. “Once we’ve done that everyone will want to be here because it’s better here. We just got to take the tax argument off the table for the production decision, and then we’ll win.” Talking to politicians from both parties, there’s always a need in interviews to navigate around their talking points and stump lines. It’s a dance: They want to stay on message, and you want to have a conversation and get some news out of it. Watch on Deadline A seasoned veteran of UK elections for Britain’s Conservative Party, Hilton is trying to sell his MAGA-lite approach out here on the very blue West Coast. Yet, unlike many of his fellow Trump-following brethren, Hilton is prepared to engage. He’s also open to saying he doesn’t know when he doesn’t have an answer, something you hear very rarely on the American campaign hustle. Perhaps that’s just a tactic of a contender behind in the polls and scratching away to be the first Republican to lead California since Arnold Schwarzenegger. Perhaps, with an eye on the next prize beyond Sacramento, it’s also a consummate operative in action. Perhaps, and most likely, it’s both and more. With a head-to-head debate coming up Wednesday night at 6 p.m. PT on CNN with his Democratic rival Xavier Becerra , Hilton took time away from the campaign trail to talk about the race and his plans. We discussed how ailing Hollywood can grow strong again, AI, the role and the reach of Trump and ICE. Hilton offered opinions on his opponent and the L.A. Mayor’s race between incumbent Karen Bass and current poll-topper Nithya Raman. Of course, this being Hollywood, the well-connected candidate also addressed the $111 billion ParaBros merger, the sudden settlement and (with a cameo by Spencer Pratt) the moves in DC toward a bipartisan federal film and TV tax credit. Getty Images DEADLINE : The first thing Steve I want to talk about is the proposed federal film and TV tax credit. This is seen, at least right now, as a bipartisan measure. Trump is obviously behind it . His arch foe Adam Schiff’s also behind it. So, strange bedfellows. California will clearly be a great beneficiary of this. With all that hype, is it possible to get this passed by the end of the year? STEVE HILTON: I think it’s very unlikely. DEADLINE : Full points for honesty. HILTON: I’d love it to get passed. I’ve been in close conversation with Jon Voight and Steven Paul, for example, and Spencer Pratt. We’re all behind it, no question. But I just don’t see the votes for it in Congress, frankly. Now I’d love it to pass. I hope I’m wrong. I sincerely hope I’m wrong, but I think that it’s unlikely to get the votes. DEADLINE: Is it unlikely to get the votes because of the strange bedfellows, or do you just think because of the calendar with the midterms and then the lame duck Congress? Is it just simply there’s just no time? HILTON: It’s mainly the calendar. DEADLINE : Really? HILTON: Also, the incorrect assumption among those who either are ignorant of the real economic realities or just don’t care and just want to pander to their own districts. DEADLINE: What do you mean by that? HILTON: I mean those who say, “Why on Earth should we be bailing out Hollywood celebrities?” I just think that’s a simple, totally false argument. But I think that it’s powerful. If you’re representing some district somewhere that has had zero connection with the entertainment industry, and that’s most districts, why would you vote for this tax credit? Why would you risk any political capital for this? Sadly, I just think it’s very unlikely. DEADLINE: I disagree, but I know that argument… HILTON: Absolutely. Which is exactly why I’ve put so much effort into making developing a really strong California package because I don’t think we can rely on the feds to come to our rescue. I don’t think we can, and so we have to save ourselves here. That’s the starting point for me. Second point is that I feel very strongly, and I say this everywhere I go, like the other week, we had a number of entertainment industry events here in L.A., roundtables with unions and others, and of course I said it to them: The mission as the next governor to me is turning around California’s business climate. DEADLINE: Why? HILTON: Because Dominic, everything is too hostile to business. All businesses, right? The litigation that you face, the energy cost, you know, all of those things: taxes, regulations, insane red tape driving business away. That’s my argument. However, I always say there are two specific industries that need emergency help right now because they are collapsing. One of them is agriculture, and the other is entertainment. They’re iconic industries for California. We have to save them. I say that to every audience, not just when I’m in L.A. County. DEADLINE: On both of those, but the entertainment industry specifically, can they be saved as we know them? HILTON: Let me say this, broadly, I agree with the argument that we shouldn’t be doing what is sometimes called a race to the bottom with tax incentives. I agree with that as an economic theory, right? But we don’t live in a world of economic theory. We live in the real world, and in the real world, that’s what’s happening. I may not love the fact that UK and Hungary and now New Jersey are doing these incredible …what you could call bribes, right, or tax incentives. But they are doing them, and so we got to compete. Xavier Becerra Getty Images DEADLINE: Secretary Becerra has not pledged he will uncap the tax credits , as you have, but everyone acknowledges that even with the state’s tax credits already at $750 million, there’s more to be done. HILTON: Agree. DEADLINE: We’ve already seen that in the last session with the post-production credit. But you’ve also talked about in your policy papers, and I read them, as this is an investment, not a handout. But to go to your earlier point, do you not worry that a federal tax incentive will lead to a race to the bottom with the UK, Canada and other countries? HILTON: I think that the difference is that we have an inherent advantage here. DEADLINE : How so? HILTON: Because people want to be here, so you have to be bribed to go elsewhere. People actually want to be in California and in L.A. particularly, and so I think we don’t have to go crazy. We just have to match the best, and we have to be as good as the best. Once we’ve done that everyone will want to be here because it’s better here. We just got to take the tax argument off the table for the production decision, and then we’ll win. DEADLINE: Speaking of winning, even though a federal judge has yet to sign off on the antitrust settlement, it looks like David Ellison will get his mega-merger. With all it took to get him and us here, what’s your stand on that, and what’s your concerns about job losses? HILTON: I see it as a long-term growth story. I mean, I haven’t particularly weighed in on it, honestly, and I’ve consciously done that because I think it’s already been politicized too much. What I do want is I want to see the industry grow, and I want to see jobs not just protected but increased. So, I do think that that means successful, profitable companies. In that sense, I trust the market process here. This should, long term, guarantee the health of the industry. That’s my sense of it. That’s why I certainly haven’t weighed in to oppose it. I’m not a cheerleader for it, but I think that it’s certainly not something that I would want to weigh in on and encourage or discourage either way. California Attorney General Rob Bonta , left, and Paramount CEO David Ellison Getty Images DEADLINE: Something or someone you have weighed in on many times in the past is California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who I believe you once called a hack. He took the lead in going after Paramount and WBD with that antitrust suit in July. He was also the one who struck a deal with Ellison earlier this month, tossing a lot of his antitrust concerns aside. HILTON: Indeed. DEADLINE: Was it political pressure from Gavin Newsom and others that caused him to back off everything? HILTON: I think the whole case was entirely political driven. I think that the substance of his case just wasn’t there. That’s why I always sensed that it was totally driven by politics, by wanting to look as if he’s sticking it to a Trump-supporting billionaire. That’s what I think this was motivated by. I mean, look at what Rob Bonta, you know, what’s his main message in his campaign for re-election? I sued the Trump administration, whatever many times. That’s his message. It’s not I’ve cracked down on crime, or I’ve made our communities safer. It’s not I’ve cracked down on the cartels or any of these other things that he could have been focusing on. It’s I sued the Trump administration. So, this is to me a proxy for that: I’m suing a Trump-supporting billionaire. DEADLINE: Were you surprised he and the 11 other blue state AGs came to a settlement with Ellison after the leaked threats that Paramount would leave LA? HILTON: No, I’m not surprised that it collapsed. Because they cobbled together some case, which was laughable when it was actually tested, in a way. I feel sorry for the other AGs that went along with it. They saw political opportunity as well, and were hoodwinked by him, I think. DEADLINE: You would be involved to some degree in all this if you win in November. There have been a lot of criticisms about the settlement. Obviously, there’s a judge in Oakland, a Biden-appointed judge, who has some very serious questions about the deal and hasn’t signed off on it yet. There’s also been an intervention by Cory Booker…. HILTON: Dominic, these people don’t know what they’re talking about. Honestly, it’s so frustrating to me. They’re just performative idiots. DEADLINE: Bonta? The judge? Booker? HILTON: David Ellison is a guy who loves this industry. David Ellison is someone who loves movies and loves this industry and loves California and loves Los Angeles. Now, I’m not sort of cheerleading for this. DEADLINE: It does sound like you are … HILTON: No, as I say, I do love Spencer and think he’s fantastic. Spencer’s been cheerleading for this, and I think that’s great, and I love that he’s done that. I’m focusing my campaign on reducing costs and get California back on track. DEADLINE: So, you don’t think you don’t think Ellison was serious when it was leaked and later confirmed that he was going to leave? You think that was negotiation? HILTON: I don’t know. I can’t see into his mind. But I know that most of the people, businesses who’ve left California, love California. They’ve just been driven out by crazy policies and hostility from the government. This was another case of that. I mean, again, it’s just obvious to me that David Ellison is someone who loves this industry and wants to make it thrive in California, and that’s great, and I agree with that. DEADLINE: Let’s see into your mind for a sec: You are behind in the polls, let’s just be honest. And with the lead Becerra has, he’s running a ghost campaign, but you are going to be with him on stage later Wednesday… HILTON: Yeah. DEADLINE: He is running a very traditional, “do no harm” campaign and you, like Andy Burnham and Trump, are taking a different way to run for office and then to govern now. HILTON: Well, I think that after all my political work, moving to America, teaching at Stanford, being involved with start-ups and then offered a new career in the media hosting on Fox News, I really feel very conscious of who I am and the working-class background I came from. And so, going to the election campaign, the parts of this that I most I most feel at home in when I’m with regular people, like really, I really like I love doing our townhalls… DEADLINE: Yes, but you are so far behind right now. There isn’t a single poll that has you even, let alone ahead. HILTON: I did Mark Halperin’s show the other day, and I made the argument to him that the polls are flawed. He kind of amplified it. He said, “Look, any you can’t do a good poll unless you have a good model of who the likely electorate is.” So, paraphrasing, right now with everything that’s going on in California, the level of dissatisfaction and turmoil, and the fact that you’re both kind of new candidates, I don’t know how you would you could predict what the electorate is in California today. That’s actually reflected in the differences in the polls. So, you have a traditional series that don’t change their assumptions about who’s going to show up and vote. Big gap, 20-points, 25-point gap, of course. Other polls that are just a bit more fine-tuned in terms of likely voters. It’s a much smaller gap, but we’re still behind. Yeah, like eight points behind, not 30 or 25. DEADLINE: To that, trying to expand your base, you have an immigrant story, but there was a blowback earlier this week to your English only in California schools remark, especially here in L.A. County, which obviously is a majority Latino county. How do you how do you factor that, knowing perfectly well that that’s going to be thrown at you in the debate? HILTON: I think it’s completely uncontroversial. Reed Hastings, for example, who is you know he’s a Democrat, he’s a great supporter of Democrats, had exactly the same position when he was chairman of the state board of education. How is anyone supposed to succeed and climb the ladder of opportunity in in California or America, for that matter, if you don’t speak English? DEADLINE: I’ll play devil’s advocate here. How could you expect to climb the ladder of opportunity in L.A. County if you don’t speak Spanish? Or to use your own words on Fox: “This is our country. We speak English here.” HILTON: In America, how are you’re going to be a startup founder if you don’t speak English? How are you going raise money on Silicon Valley’s Sand Hill Road? It’s insulting and it’s patronizing, and it’s exactly why right now you have a total crisis of literacy with huge numbers not proficient in English. It’s a total disaster. Anti-ICE protests during “National Shutdown” on January 30, 2026 in Los Angeles DEADLINE: You have been very clear that you are you are a supporter of Donald Trump. So, do you feel that what we have seen with the immigration raids and abductions – especially with American citizens have been plucked off the street and kids plucked off the streets, put in detention centers, sent to overseas – how do you factor that into your campaign, and how do you factor that into being governor? HILTON: It’s nothing compared to what Xavier Becerra did when he was Secretary of Health and Human Services under Biden sending thousands and thousands of Latino children directly into the hands of child sex and labor traffickers. DEADLINE: Whoa… HILTON: As a result of his personal decisions, in order to try and launder his reputation, because he didn’t like the TV pictures of kids in camps that he was responsible for, because he was so utterly incompetent. So instead of actually dealing with the problem, he dismantled the checks and the vetting for where these children should be sent, That was his job, because he was responsible for the Office of Refugee Resettlement. That’s under HHS. Today, there are still over 300,000 missing, unaccounted for. Some of them may have aged out of the system. They may have returned to the country they came from. We don’t know. What we do know is that of that number, because their ages are recorded when they came across the border, 100,000 are under 10 today. DEADLINE: The numbers of lost and abandoned children may differ, but what happened at HHS under Becerra is undeniably heartbreaking. It’s also a big part of this campaign. But, in the context of two wrongs don’t make a right, I feel like you’re dodging my question about Trump and ICE in California. HILTON: Well, I’m very happy to talk about it. Let’s break it down. First of all, a lot of this is their refusal to just engage in normal legal cooperation under California’s sanctuary state law. There’s no reason for this this confrontational attitude with immigration enforcement. It’s entirely political and performative. All of this drama and confrontation and rage has been created entirely by Democrat politicians. DEADLINE: Steve, you can’t honestly say that you don’t think that the administration has taken a very confrontational approach. If you just take them on their initial word that they were going to arrest criminals, and what they are doing is hauling children, families of service members and legal American citizens into detention camps … HILTON: If they, well, if you look, what they say about that is, and first of all… DEADLINE: I’m asking what you say as the Republican candidate for governor about that. What you would say to the people of L.A. who live in fear, who have seen family members taken? HILTON: (PAUSES) I’ll tell you what I would do, which is lower the temperature on this whole issue. As governor, I know all the people involved, and I will get on the phone, meet in person, and say, right, we need to sort this out. I don’t want to see any of this going on in California. Let’s focus on what the priorities are and work together calmly and cooperatively to make that happen, which is to focus on the people that, where there’s a broad consensus, should be removed from the country. DEADLINE Which are? HILTON: Illegal immigrants who’ve committed some other kind of crime, especially violent crime. Let’s work on that together. That’s what I would do. So, I’m not really interested in so much in you know commenting on what’s happened in the past, I’m just telling you what I would actually do as governor, which is to lower the temperature, work together within the sanctuary state law to focus on removing the people who most Californians would agree shouldn’t be here. All the time you’re hearing these stories of crimes committed by people who everyone agrees should not be here, but judges are releasing them. Local law enforcement is releasing them, not notifying immigration enforcement, and they go back into the community, and that’s happening all the time. This whole argument is broken as far as I’m concerned. Gavin Newsom Getty Images DEADLINE: On a much less human scale, at least for now, another argument that some people feel is broken is artificial intelligence or superintelligence, as Trump likes to call it. There are a lot of concerns, especially because the hub of AI in this country is here in California. This is what we have created in many ways. Newsom has put in what he says are various safeguards and guardrails that are going to protect people and institutions. If they’re even effective, they only go as far as the state line. With all the doom and gloom, even from the CEOs themselves, what do you think needs to be done with AI?. HILTON: Yeah, I think it’s a huge question, and we got to take it very seriously. I think that we’re leading, and I want us to continue to lead. That’s the first point. I want us to continue to lead this incredible industry, just as we’ve led so many others. I want to keep it here in California, not drive it away, which is what current policies would do. So that’s the first point. And the second point, I actually want to see more of it here? DEADLINE: More AI? HILTON: Pretty much all the job creation from this new wave of technology is happening in other states. The high-end manufacturing, construction, infrastructure, all in Texas, Nevada, Arizona, elsewhere. You saw Nvidia, fantastic Bay Area success story last year announced a half trillion-dollar investment in America, none of it in California. Like, can we please have the jobs and investment from this industry here rather than chasing it out to other states? That’s a very important point. On that question of regulation, I think there’s some easier and harder questions here. One of them is protecting children. I don’t think we’re doing enough at the moment. It’s all very haphazard and random. It’s being rolled out in ways that are just, I think, very dangerous. You know, 11 years ago, I wrote a book, More Human, arguing that children shouldn’t have smartphones. I think the Australia ban is a waste of time because it’s not aiming at the real target, which is the device. It’s not the apps. It’s the device, the smartphone. That’s the problem. We’ve got to get smartphones out of kids’ lives. Also, there’s way too much involvement of the tech companies in in core academic processes like setting curriculum and so on. That’s been really corrupt and that’s got to end. Secondly, I think we had we need an immediate pause on AI in the classroom. Immediate. I think that L.A. Unified has done that, and I agree with that. And I want to see that statewide. Not for long, right? Just a pause while we actually evaluate how and if, if and how we want AI to be used in education. There’s very concerning reporting of what what’s being described as cognitive stunting, where you have the introduction of AI too early, and it’s actually changing kids’ ability to think. So I think that shouldn’t be a difficult thing to get agreement on. DEADLINE : Except if you are a tech company… HILTON: Yes DEADLINE: On Wednesday night you’re going to be meeting your opponent, Secretary Beccera. It might be the only time you actually get face to face with him before November. CNN are hosting this with Jake Tapper and Dana Bash moderating. There’s going to be a lot of topics that we’ve discussed here coming up like the film industry, tax credits, and Paramount Warner Bros merger. You’re a seasoned television performer, how did you prepare for this debate? HILTON: What I’ve been doing the last year and a half, honestly. Traveling the state, meeting people, understanding what’s going on, and responding to their questions. That’s the true answer. I’ve been preparing for five years for this debate with the work I‘ve been doing is what I would say to that. DEADLINE: I’m not throwing any shade on you at all but let’s assume the polls are correct, and you don’t win. What are you going to do next? HILTON: I don’t know. I really haven’t thought about it. I really haven’t. DEADLINE: Steve? HILTON: I swear, all my thought process is, “How are we going to start?” You know what comes first? I’m thinking its very important to establish a good relationship with the leaders of the legislature. That’s going to be crucial. I want to make, you know, phone them straight away. Let’s get together, the mayors of the big cities. You know we got to work together. We got to solve some problems… Los Angeles City Councilmember Nithya Raman, left, and Mayor Karen Bass Apu Gomes / JC Olivera / David McNew / Getty Images DEADLINE: Let me ask you then, because you brought up big cities, who’s going to be the next mayor of L.A.? HILTON: It’s hard to tell, but it seems to me like the momentum is with Nithya, doesn’t it? I think that there’s some justice in that. DEADLINE: Why? HILTON: Whatever one may think of Nithya Raman or Karen Bass, and I haven’t met either of them, so I’m really not judging, and I’m not weighing in. I don’t have a vote in LA. But I do think that there’s something about rewarding the level of failure that Karen Bass has presided over that’s very hard for voters to do that. My attitude is also I’m going to have to work with either of them, and I’m looking forward to working with either of them, you know, to make things happen. Especially in L.A., it’s a hugely important relationship because we got the Olympics coming up. I mean, it’s just like an absolutely central thing that we got to get right. DEADLINE : Is to get things right why you are running? HILTON : (LAUGHS) Truly I’m running because I love California. The reason I felt so at home here, as soon as we got here, and wanted to stay here and be here and be part of the story of California, is that I love it. It’s not just the physical beauty and the weather and all those things we can see and touch, but there’s the soul and a spirit of California that is just so precious. DEADLINE: I hear a stump speech starting… HILTON: Truly, I think that’s what’s being crushed by what’s happened over 16 years of this one-party rule. The spirit of California is the rebel spirit, I often call it, and we got this government that’s just so weighing us down. We’ve got so much potential, and we can, you know, do anything, build anything, make anything, grow anything. We don’t. You just need the government to get its basic things right, and then Californians will do the rest. I don’t want to tell people how to live their life. DEADLINE: All politicians do, especially the ones who say they don’t. HILTON: I really don’t. I want everyone to have the chance to live the life they want in a way that’s affordable and safe and secure. Go about their business and have a fantastic time in this incredible state of ours. That’s all I’m here to do. Believe it or not, this interview has been edited for length and clarity. title: ‘Final Payment’, ‘Congo Boy’ Win Top Awards At Pingyao International Film Festival
full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz ‘Final Payment’, ‘Congo Boy’ Win Top Awards At Pingyao International Film Festival Iran’s Mohammad Rasoulof & Japanese-Korean Filmmaker Mipo O To Receive Kurosawa Akira Award At Tokyo Film Festival ‘The Assassin(s)’ Tops Korea’s Chuseok Holiday Box Office With 1.5 Million Admissions View All September 29, 2026 8:56pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Closing ceremony of Pingyao International Film Festival 2026 PYIFF Chinese director Niu Niu’s Final Payment scooped the Best Film Award in the Fei Mu Awards of this year’s Pingyao International Film Festival (PYIFF), while Rafiki Fariala’s Congo Boy won Best Film in the festival’s Roberto Rossellini Awards. Final Payment , which also won Best Actor for Niu Jianrong’s performance, revolves around a homeowner clashing with a contractor over the final payment following a set of renovations on his home. PYIFF’s competition jury stated: “Tearing through a very small rip, the film leads us into a reality and emotional landscape so expansive, where we sigh, lament, and reflect. The director’s approach is concise, unpretentious, and masterful, earning the wholehearted recognition of the entire jury.” Related Stories News Pingyao Film Festival Unveils 10th Edition Line-up; 'Spring In A Small Town' Set As Opening Film News Cannes Un Certain Regard Winners: Sandra Wollner's 'Everytime' Takes Top Prize The Best Film award came with a cash prize of $150,000 (RMB1m) with half given to the director for the development of their next film, and half given to the distributor in China. Niu Niu previously directed Mr Junjun , which was awarded with the Jury Award and Youth Jury Award at PYIFF in 2023. Watch on Deadline Also in the Fei Mu Awards, Xu Zao won Best Director for Light Pillar , while Best Actress went to Sun Yi for Wang Xiaozhen’s A Joke . The Jury Award was presented to Dong Jie’s Zoom In, Zoom Out , which had its world premiere in Venice Critics Week, while a special mention went to Cai Chengjie’s Suzhou Quarte t. The Fei Mu awards are focused on the festival’s Hidden Dragons section, which selects first, second and third films from emerging directors making Chinese-language films, while the Roberto Rossellini Awards focus on the Crouching Tigers section for emerging international directors. Congo Boy, which took Best Film in the Roberto Rossellini Awards, also won Best Actor when it premiered in Un Certain Regard at this year’s Cannes film festival. The PYIFF award came with a cash prize of $20,000, with half given to the director for the development of their next film, and half given to the distributor in China. The PYIFF jury stated: “The Jury unanimously has been moved by this autobiographical story, told in a simple style that echoes the great tradition of neorealism. For a film focusing on a character that confronts his world with optimism despite dark times and takes on his shoulders the destiny of his entire family.” Also in this section, the Philippines’ Rafael Manuel won Best Director for Filipiñan a, while the Jury Award went to Ben’imana , directed by Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo, which won the Camera d’Or at this year’s Cannes. The PYIFF jury also awarded Rakan Mayasi’s Yesterday The Eye Didn’t Sleep a Special Mention. Hong Kong filmmaker Ann Hui received the Crouching Tiger Hidden Dragon East-West Award, shortly before she receives the Camellia Award at Busan International Film Festival next week. Pingyao’s International Contribution To Chinese Cinema Award went to Marco Müller, who founded the festival with Chinese auteur Jia Zhangke and currently serves as Artistic Director of the Film Art Research Centre at Shanghai University, and veteran producer, director and former chairman of China Film Group Han Sanping. Hello Group chairman Tang Yan was presented with a 10th Anniversary Award. This year’s PYIFF opened on September 24 with a screening of the 4K restoration of Fei Mu’s Spring In A Small Town ; closed with Good Trip , co-directed by Hong Kong filmmakers Norris Wong and Hoi Wong, and also screened Jia’s short film Torino Shadow , which premiered at this year’s Cannes. PINGYAO INTERNATIONAL FILM FESTIVAL 2026 AWARDS: FEI MU AWARDS: Best Film: Final Payment , dir: Niu Niu Best Director: Xu Zao, Light Pillar Best Actress: Sun Yi, A Joke , dir: Wang Xiaozhen Best Actor: Niu Jianrong, Final Payment , dir: Niu Niu Jury Award: Zoom In, Zoom Out , dir: Dong Jie Special Mention: Suzhou Quartet , dir: Cai Chengjie ROBERTO ROSSELLINI AWARDS: Best Film: Congo Boy , dir: Rafiki Fariala Best Director: Filipiñana , dir: Rafael Manuel Jury Award: Ben’imana , dir: Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo Special Mention: Yesterday The Eye Didn’t Sleep , dir: Rakan Mayasi BBC Studios Scripted Boss Jamie Hall On Talent Deal Strategy Zygi Kamasa’s True Brit UK Distributor Files For Administration Anton Backs Romain Bessi’s Indie Alliance The Creatives Paramount Streaming Boss Cindy Holland Exiting Ahead Of WBD Merger Read More About: Comments

title: ‘Ted Lasso’ Pays Tribute To Anthony Head – Here’s Why It Happened In Episode 409
full_text: Skip to main content By Nellie Andreeva Nellie Andreeva Editor-In-Chief @DeadlineNellie More Stories By Nellie ‘Ted Lasso’ Pays Tribute To Anthony Head – Here’s Why It Happened In Episode 409 Cindy Holland Leaving Paramount Ahead Of WBD Merger ‘Spider-Man’ Sony Universe TV Series Based On Clone Saga Marvel Comics Storyline Nears Amazon Green Light View All September 30, 2026 12:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Anthony Head in "Ted Lasso" Apple TV+. SPOILER ALERT: The story includes details about Episodes 408 and 409 of Apple TV’s Ted Lasso . A very emotional Ted Lasso episode that included the death of a beloved original character, The Crown & Anchor pub owner Mae Green, played by Annette Badland, also acknowledged the death of the series’ popular recurring cast member Anthony Head , who played the villainous Rupert Mannion in the first three seasons. A card, In Memory of Anthony Head, ran at the end of Season 4’s penultimate episode, “Mae Rides the Bus.” (You can see it below.) Related Stories News Anthony Head Dies: ‘Ted Lasso’ & ‘Buffy The Vampire Slayer’ Actor Was 72 News ‘Ted Lasso’ Season 4 Shocker: Actor Reflects On Death Of OG Character Who “Went In The Very Best Way” “He was a beautiful man, and he will be much missed,” Badland told Deadline during an interview about Mae’s shocking death , reminiscing about famous Season 1 darts scene between Rupert and Jason Sudeikis’ Ted Lasso at Mae’s pub. “He was charming and funny and generous, and we’d have naughty little sort of asides. Ted Lasso was always expected to pay tribute to the veteran British actor who died on June 1 at the age of 72 . When that was not done in the Season 4 premiere, many thought that Head would be honored in an episode he appears in as the season had wrapped production in January, months before his passing. “I assumed he would be in this last [season], and didn’t know, as I think very few people knew, he was ill and just couldn’t do it,” Badland said. Barely referenced in the first seven episodes, Head’s Rupert, ex-owner of AFC Richmond and ex-husband of the club’s current owner Rebecca (Hannah Waddingham), came back into the forefront in Episode 8, when Higgins (Jeremy Swift), with the help of Mae and her “Follow the anger” advice, deducted that Rupert had been secretly buying shares to regain control of Richmond. That remained a story thread in Episode 9 until the surprise twist at the end that revealed it was not Rupert but Tracey Ullman’s Zelda Southport who was behind the shady operation and on the verge of becoming a majority owner of the club. The move raised questions whether Ted Lasso had pivoted from Rupert to Zelda as the culprit — and away from a potential Rebecca vs. Rupert battle for control of Richmond — in light of Head’s death (or leading into it). According to sources, no Season 4 storylines were changed following Head’s passing, there had been no formal plans for Head to be in Season 4 and no official approach to him about appearing. It is unclear whether that was related to Head’s health issues which had been kept private. (His cause of death was listed by his daughters as complications due to pneumonia.) Head’s last acting credits were Season 3 of Ted Lasso, which came out in 2023, and the 2024 Prime Video movie Upgraded. It is a longstanding TV tradition for characters to mirror the death of the actors who played them by passing away in the show. Because of the timing of Head’s passing after Season 4 had been completed, that will likely happen in Season 5, which has not been picked up yet but is looking good. ‘Ted Lasso’s Rupert-Zelda Switch The eccentric ultra-wealthy entrepreneur and sports investor Zelda — a polarizing and largely disliked new character introduced in Season 4 — had long been suspected by fans to be the season’s secret villain. Zelda, who had become involved in Richmond’s women’s team with Keeley’s (Juno Temple) enthusiastic support over Rebecca’s serious reservations, was present when Higgins told Rebecca in Season 8 that Rupert was behind the buyouts. In fact, Zelda looked rather nervous for a moment when Higgins announced that he had solved the mystery before he dropped Rupert’s name and she chimed in with “Never underestimate the power of anger as fuel.” (We will likely find out more about her motives in the Season 4 finale.) In Episode 9, Zelda also happened to be there any time Higgins and Rebecca discussed the matter. That included him telling his boss in the office that Rupert’s lawyers were “denying knowing anything about people selling shares but since there has been a pause in buying” and that Rebecca won’t lose control of the club regardless, as long as the Milk sisters, who no one had been able to get ahold of, don’t sell their shares. The three also were together on board the Richmond private jet when Higgins told Rebecca that even without the Milk sisters, the mystery buyer they believed to be Rupert can get 49% of the shares. That may prove a moot point as Zelda was later seen giving her henchman, who had located the sisters, instructions to go as high as needed to secure their shares. With the mystery solved, the producers felt it made sense to run an end card honoring Head in Season 9. Rupert had his Season 4 moment in 408 and 409, so paying tribute to Head following the close of his character’s two-episode arc felt most appropriate. (Running the card at the end of Episode 8 likely also would’ve spoiled the surprise that it wasn’t Rupert who was buying the shares.) Head recurred on the first two seasons of Ted Lasso, becoming a series regular in Season 3. His character Rupert, Rebecca’s vindictive and philandering former husband who lost Richmond to her in the divorce, was the original three-season installment’s main antagonist. He subsequently bought another Premiere League team — West Ham United — and recruited Ted’s kitman turned assistant coach Nathan Shelley (Nick Mohammed) to work with him, before losing it in the Season 3 finale. “We will miss him, I respect him, and it’s a great honor to be in the episode that is dedicated to him,” Badland said. title: Channel 4 Teaming With Stroke Association On Doc Series Spotlighting Young People Recovering From Strokes
full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart , Jesse Whittock September 30, 2026 1:26am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Trauma: My Broken Brain' Stream Media Group EXCLUSIVE: Channel 4 is teaming with the Stroke Association on a documentary sereis looking at young people living with the aftermath of a stroke. Trauma: My Broken Brain follows three young survivors through the most frightening days of their lives and the grueling journey back to independence. Every five minutes someone in the UK suffers a stroke – there are 1.4 million stroke survivors living in the UK today – but the aim of the doc is to show that this is only the beginning of recovery. Filmed over a year with access to these young adults at the most terrifying and testing moments of their lives, the series meets Dan (28), a dancer left confined to a wheelchair, barely able to speak following emergency brain surgery; Saskia (22), a self-described social butterfly left bedbound after a brain bleed so severe her family feared she would not survive; and Dec (20), who collapsed just four months into a new relationship and spent weeks in a coma, his family and girlfriend unsure if he would survive. It is being produced by Stream Media Group , which was also behind the same network’s Anna Richardson: Love, Loss and Dementia , made with the Alzheimer’s Society. Watch on Deadline Channel 4 commissoning exec Simon Lee said: “This is an ambitious and important series that challenges perceptions and gives a voice to young people whose lives have been transformed by stroke, as they embark on the long road that begins after survival.” Stream’s Victoria Noble added: “What struck us throughout filming was how little people understand about stroke. Survival is often seen as the end of the story, when in reality, it is only the beginning. By sharing their journeys with such honesty and courage, Dec, Dan and Saskia revealed the reality of rebuilding a life after stroke, and the truth behind the long and unforgiving journey to reclaim the right to live an independent life. Alongside the extraordinary support of their families, their stories offer a powerful insight into resilience, determination and hope. It’s been a privilege to tell their stories.” Noble is EP with Ben Padfield and producer is Laura Hooper. Series director is Storm Theunissen and production executive is Fiona Ridgers. The show was filmed with access to The Walton Centre NHS Foundation Trust and Clatterbridge Rehabilitation Centre, and Wirral University Teaching Hospital NHS Foundation Trust. title: BBC Studios Scripted Boss Spotlights Strategy Behind Indie & Talent Deals: “We’re Not Going To Spend Millions Buying A Production Company”
full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max ‘Doctor Who’: Multiple BBC Studios Labels Likely To Apply For Tender Callum Scott Howells & Gabrielle Creevy Leading Adaptation Of Vanessa Savage Thriller ‘The Night They Vanished’ For BBC Studios & Channel 4 BBC Studios Scripted Boss Spotlights Strategy Behind Indie & Talent Deals: “We’re Not Going To Spend Millions Buying A Production Company” View All September 30, 2026 2:00am Add us as a Google Preferred Source Clockwise Top L-R: Honey, Doctor Who, Alice and Steve, Ann Droid (inst) Jamie Hall BBC Studios/Bad Wolf/James Pardon/Hulu EXCLUSIVE: BBC Studios ’ scripted chief has laid out his strategy for future indie and talent investments that will shy away from “going out and spending £20M ($26.5M) on a production company.” Speaking exclusively with Deadline for his first interview since taking on the Scripted MD role, Jamie Hall said his plan for the Doctor Who , Baby Reindeer and Sherwood maker is instead to strike smaller but more regular deals with top talent and “build creative hubs.” In this vein, Hall said BBC Studios scripted will “move slightly closer” to the strategy of soon-to-be-independent rival ITV Studios. Related Stories Executives BBC Studios Names Mediawan's Sally Habbershaw President Of Global Distribution News 'Doctor Who' Re-Gen Is Go! BBC Calls On Producers To Pitch "Brave" New Vision For Sci-Fi Series Hall came to our interview clutching receipts in the shape of two new labels led by the producers behind Strike and The Detection Club , along with early-stage plans for a label that will focus on digital spin-offs of existing brands. Watch on Deadline BBC Studios runs hefty in-house drama and comedy teams along with majority-owning big beasts of the UK production world like Baby Reindeer maker Clerkenwell Films, Sherwood producer House Productions, Lookout Point and Steve Coogan’s Baby Cow. Hall joined earlier this year , three decades on from his first stint at the BBC (he met his wife working on Our Friends in the North ) from Vice Studios/Pulse Films, where he oversaw the likes of Gangs Of London. At BBC Studios, his remit is to give a shot in the arm to the drama and comedy offering and unearth the next generation of IP at a time when the public service BBC is desperate for funding. His desire echoes that of his boss, BBC Studios Productions chief Zai Bennett, which is to invest in around two to three of these new-look talent labels per year. Other examples include tie-ups with Barbie star Jamie Demetriou, The Ballad of Wallis Island writer Tom Basden, Ted Lasso alum Nick Mohammed and Cunk on Earth creator Diane Morgan. “I inherited a group of great production companies that had been acquired in the way production companies were acquired at the time,” Hall told Deadline from BBC Studios’ Soho outpost. “But I don’t think the market can support that anymore – or, at least, it can only do so very rarely. We’re not going to spend £20 million buying a production company. Instead, we’re building an amazing service at the center of the studio, then creating creative hubs that can tap into our brilliant lawyers, HR, finance and other support functions.” Hall didn’t completely rule out stumping up big bucks to buy an indie outright in the future, but added: “The reality is that I can set up creative pods or labels at a much lower price point, and that feels right.” He said the scripted supremo role at BBC Studios had attracted him because, “I wasn’t simply coming in to mind the wheel. There was a creative renewal that needed to happen – some wiring and plumbing that needed fixing.” Backing up his strategy, Hall unveiled Bristol-based Landed Productions led by Strike and Possession producer Jenny van der Lande, who is leaving her role as Big Talk’s creative director of drama to helm BBC Studios’ first scripted label outside London. Landed Productions will make “premium genre pieces” and van der Lande has multiple writers in mind with whom she wants to develop shows. “Jenny said in our conversations that she doesn’t want to run a production company,” explained Hall. “She wants to work with amazing writers she already has relationships with, then partner up when she gets a greenlight.” Hall’s new-look team, which consists of the likes of CFO Jennifer Dickson, legal chief Anna Beese and production director Alison Loose, has also been busy working on the digital spin-offs label that follows big digital successes for franchises like Dancing with the Stars and EastEnders . This one, which doesn’t yet have a name, will be led by BBC Studios Drama digital chief Katy Karger. “Scripted is probably the hardest area to crack [in digital], so we’re setting up a central digital capability,” said Hall. “When someone pitches a conventional piece of television, we can also pitch to buyers a digital component.” Hall also unveiled CliffEdge Entertainment, led by “real grafter” Deborah Sathe, who is moving across from her role as Senior Creative Director at the in-house BBC Studios Drama Productions. CliffEdge will take some shows off Drama Productions’ hands such as The Detection Club, Silent Witness, Father Brown and Shakespeare and Hathaway , while the Kate Oates-run Drama Productions will continue making soaps and continuing drama. Some staff will move over to CliffEdge. “When I came in, I spent a lot of time getting to know all the creatives in the business and Deb Sathe was one of the people who really impressed me with her energy and what she was building,” added Hall. “She’s a real grafter, but is also incredibly disciplined about making shows at a certain price point. It felt natural for her to have her own entity to run.” CliffEdge comes replete with a greenlight: an adaptation of Vanessa Savage’s gripping thriller The Night They Vanished starring It’s a Sin’s Callum Scott Howells and Gabrielle Creevy ( Black Doves ). That one has been pre-bought by Channel 4 and follows Anna (Creevy), whose world is blown apart when she discovers her childhood house listed on a true crime website as the scene of her family’s future deaths. Intriguing blind date Cai (Scott Howells) runs the true-crime site, but he swears he didn’t post it. “I’ve done the rounds of most of the agencies” The Night They Vanished speaks to what Hall believes BBC Studios can do with big IP. He says he has “done the rounds of most of the agencies to remind them that we’re open” – the day after he chats with Deadline he has a meeting in the diary with Curtis Brown – and is in talks over “a number of pieces of IP that are coming through which are quite interesting.” Driven by the success of Sky and AMC’s Gangs of London, for which he says Pulse was “a bit ahead of the curve,” Hall is chatting to rightsholders about the possibility of revamping in-vogue gaming IP for the small screen. This follows big successes for the likes of HBO’s The Last of Us. Although none of these examples are necessarily franchise-able in the vein of a Gangs of London or Doctor Who, Hall reels off a list of upcoming BBC Studios shows he is buzzing for, including the BBC’s Killing Eve origin story Honey , Netflix surfing drama Breakers and a second season of Disney+ rom-com Alice and Steve. Another hit dominating ratings at the moment is Diane Morgan’s comedy Ann Droid , which poignantly taps into societal paranoia about AI but in an oh-so-gentle way. Having yesterday become the BBC’s biggest new scripted comedy since Ludwig Season 1, Hall reveals there is “real interest” in Ann Droid from American buyers, who are familiar with Morgan from her work as comedy creation Philomena Cunk and could either buy finished tape or commission their own unique version. Hall has plenty experience working for American behemoths and will soon sit down with BBC Studios’ new L.A. chief Ryan O’Dowd to figure out “how we can be better joined up, because inevitably our producers [in the UK] want access to the U.S. market.” This comes at a time when Hall says the co-pro market is “picking up a bit” from the lows of 2025 , although he acknowledges it is “nowhere near what it was in the past and there is still quite a big oversupply in the market of producers and projects.” “If we’re designing a show and the budget is at a [higher] level then we need to start thinking about [co-pros] much earlier in the process,” he added. “What has happened in the past is you develop a show for [BBC drama boss] Lindsay [Salt] and she says she wants it and then you go, ‘Oh crap we can’t finance it with just Lindsay and the tax credit, we need co-pro’. But by then the show has been developed in such a distinct way.” He hopes his experience in the belly of the beast at Vice can help but is so far loving being part of a public service machine, which Hall labels the fourth biggest brand in the world. “Our ultimate owner is the epitome of patient money,” he said. “Whereas when I was at Vice it was owned by three American banks and if we didn’t hit our numbers each quarter we were in trouble.” This unique BBC model helps in the current landscape, Hall reckons, coming as the Banijay-All3Media mega-merger marches on. “I imagine that if you’ve got a super-indie with 130 production companies, the amount of facetime you’re going to have with the boss is quite minimal,” he added. “What I really lean into is the way we’re structured. Zai [Bennett] and I sit opposite each other, across a bank of desks. We don’t have to wait for L.A. to wake up before we make a decision; we can just get on with things.” “Just getting on with things” is a crucial mantra for a BBC Studios scripted operation that is feeling more and more pressure to return funds to the cash-strapped 100-year-old national broadcaster . Is Hall feeling the pressure? “There’s no denying that any headwinds the BBC faces will come and hit us,” he added. “All I can do is manage that and focus on where we can grow our business outside of that [traditional BBC funding] route to help compensate. The BBC gets beat up so much. What we can do inside the studio is really help it and support it.” CA Gov Candidate Steve Hilton On Federal Tax Credits, ParaBros Merger & More ‘Ted Lasso’ Shocker: Actor Reflects On Death Of OG Character BBC Studios Scripted Boss Jamie Hall On Talent Deal Strategy Review & Red Carpet Premiere Photos With Anne Hathaway, Dakota Johnson Read More About: Comments

title: ‘Doctor Who’: Multiple BBC Studios Labels Likely To Apply For Tender
full_text: Skip to main content By Max Goldbart Max Goldbart International TV Co-Editor @Goldbart1 More Stories By Max ‘Doctor Who’: Multiple BBC Studios Labels Likely To Apply For Tender Callum Scott Howells & Gabrielle Creevy Leading Adaptation Of Vanessa Savage Thriller ‘The Night They Vanished’ For BBC Studios & Channel 4 BBC Studios Scripted Boss Spotlights Strategy Behind Indie & Talent Deals: “We’re Not Going To Spend Millions Buying A Production Company” View All September 30, 2026 2:30am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Doctor Who' BBC Studios/Bad Wolf/James Pardon EXCLUSIVE: At least one BBC Studios indie will be throwing its hat in the ring to become the next producer of Doctor Who , with scripted boss Jamie Hall telling Deadline he “firmly believes” the entire BBC group should “reap the rewards” of the iconic sci-fi series. Hall said “we’ve probably got one, potentially two companies” going for the multi-million pound tender, which if successful would bring the show back in house following two seasons made by Sony-owned Bad Wolf, starring Ncuti Gatwa. His comments followed BBC Studios CEO Tom Fussell recently saying BBC Studios would be applying “with gusto.” Related Stories News BBC Studios Scripted Boss Spotlights Strategy Behind Indie & Talent Deals: "We're Not Going To Spend Millions Buying A Production Company" News Graham Norton Says It's Getting Harder To Launch Talk Shows: "I Feel Like We Might End Up Being The Last Chat Show On Planet Earth" Hall wouldn’t reveal the names of the indies but said he would “100%” be happy for more than one to enter the race. Watch on Deadline BBC Studios runs an in-house drama label, which made Doctor Who before Bad Wolf, while it also owns several scripted indies outright including Baby Reindeer maker Clerkenwell Films, Happy Valley producer Lookout Point and Sherwood indie House Productions. While he hasn’t seen his labels’ proposals, Hall said he has been “very open” and honest with those keen to go for the tender because the process is “quite an onerous undertaking and costs quite a bit of money.” “I have to make sure that it doesn’t become a distraction from the day job,” he added. If two BBC Studios labels enter, they will likely join Line of Duty producer World Productions, whose boss Simon Heath has previously indicated his ITV Studios-owned outfit is interested. More thoughts from producers can be found in our future Doctor Who analysis from over the summer. Published a fortnight ago, the tender calls for a “relevant, surprising, brave and inspiring” new vision for the show that should premiere in 2028-29. Notably, it said it is happy for indies to pitch a series using “episodic writers” rather than a “showrunner model,” which would do away with how Doctor Who has been made in recent years. After several years with Bad Wolf and after the termination of the just-ended Disney+ co-pro deal , Hall was adamant that Doctor Who “should sit within the BBC and the whole group should reap the rewards of it.” Questioned on what he would want to see from a revamped Doctor Who, Hall harked back to the days when Matt Smith and David Tennant were playing the Doctor. “It feels to me that there is an opportunity to get back to what the core offering was in that time,” he added. “It will be off screen for two or three years and that gives the audience a great chance to have a break then rediscover, while also bringing a new audience.” CA Gov Candidate Steve Hilton On Federal Tax Credits, ParaBros Merger, More Red Carpet Premiere Photo Gallery, Anne Hathaway, Dakota Johnson, Review BBC Studios Scripted Boss Jamie Hall On Talent Deal Strategy Paramount Streaming Boss Cindy Holland Exiting Ahead Of WBD Merger Read More About: Comments

full_text: Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Fremantle International Commercial Strategy VP Jill Kellie Exits After Four Years ‘Joseph’s Machines’, ‘Triple Charm’ & ‘What’s Up Moms’ Among Volt Factor Shows Rolling Out On Future Today Channels Hearst Networks UK Buys ‘American Chopper’ Revival Series ‘Orange County Choppers Original’ View All September 30, 2026 2:32am Add us as a Google Preferred Source 'Lock Upp' Netflix Netflix is returning the inmates to the Lock Upp jail. What broke through with audiences was some of the more divisive characters discussing their public perception and confronting narratives that have surrounded them. Watch on Deadline Netflix said Season 2 “build on that world, bringing audiences back inside the jail for another chapter where personalities collide, dynamics shift, and every secret has the potential to change the game.” Riteish Deshmukh and Farah Khan return as hosts, with Balaji Telefilms producing. Show creator Ekta Kapoor is producing alongside Shobha Kapoor and Manisha Sharma, with Malaya Pradhan the showrunner. “ Lock Upp: Sach Yaa Sazaa became appointment viewing overnight,” said Monika Shergill, VP of Content at Netflix India. “Viewers invested, debated, and kept coming back. It captured the zeitgeist — not just as entertainment, but also as a space where celebrities talked about topics they rarely do, owned their choices and confronted past trauma. “Ekta’s bold homegrown idea and the scaled adaptation on Netflix led to entertainment maxxing. Season 2 will be about recreating the same Netflix effect with many new surprises for our audiences.” Ekta Kapoor, Jjoint Managing Director at Balaji, added: “ Lock Upp: Sach Ya Sazaa on Netflix went far beyond what we imagined. The conversations, the inmates, and their most memorable moments continued to live with audiences even after the finale. That’s what makes the return of Lock Upp so exciting. “The next season will take audiences back into a world they know, but with an entirely new set of stories, personalities, and surprises. And Farah and Riteish will continue to helm the Lock Upp as the formidable jailer duo, bringing their own energy, unpredictability, and dynamic to the next chapter.” Lock Upp originally launched on ALTBalaji and MX Player in 2022, but was rebooted for Netflix.
